text: D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
ru_trans: Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает более двадцати видов обуви, встречающихся в трех романах Соколова: “*башмаки, ботфорты, боты, ботинки (полуботинки), чеботы, чизмы, чубуры, галоши (калоши), геты, ичиги, кеды, клоги, лапти, мокроступы, обуви (обувки), сапоги, сандалии, тапочки (полутапочки), шлепанцы, штиблеты, тапти, туфли, валенки*. Список можно расширить, включив такие атрибуты, как носки, чулки, портянки, гамаши, коньки, костыли и протезы” (Johnson “The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). text: Double meaning, very relevant from a thematic point of view for the plot: 1. hunting / 2. desire. The quote is from B. Pasternak, *Doctor Zhivago*, part 5, chapter 14. It is also interesting to notice that in Pasternak's novel this “young man” is the interlocutor with whom Zhivago converses while on the train: "Once in the dark of the night, the interlocutor turns out to be deaf and, therefore, capable of sustaining a conversation solely by lip reading. This pivotal sequence in Pasternak’s novel unravels the theme of incommunicability, a topic that is of great interest to Sokolov too. By evoking the idea of the power of language and of its sound, which not everyone is capable of hearing, Sokolov once again stresses the redeeming sacredness of the word. After all, this seemingly epistolary second novel by Sokolov presents itself as a letter addressed to detective Pozhilykh by Ilya Zynzyrela (later discovered to be dead), in which the sender seeks justice for a wrongdoing. Thus, the writing offers a refuge and a redemption from (linear) time and death" (Napolitano, Sasha Sokolov 88). Elena Kravchenko also writes, "The unsettling feeling, triggered by the man's intense gaze, overly articulate speech, and lapses into occasional withdrawals, is explained next day. He is deaf, and in order to hear and therefore speak, he needs to see and read the lips of his collocutor. By virtue of his link with Pasternak's hunter, Iakov can be associated with the visual aspect of language. It is also reflected in his artistic aspirations, manifested in the 'picture gallery' of the prose section" (*Reflections *81).

text: The title of Ilya's chapters derives from the Tatar name of the Volga river (Itil'), and recalls the *[Zadonshchina](http://www.drevne.ru/lib/zadon_s.htm)*, an epic literary text (dated late 14th century) about the Battle of Kulikovo of 1380 (its title derives from the river Don). As "the Zadonshchina shows the humanity of the Tatar troops and expresses genuine sympathy for a grief the Russian and Tatar alike could understand” (Halperin, *The Golden Horde *109), the Zaitil'shchina describes the diverse human universe by the Volga (Zavol'zhe), or Wolf river (Zavol'che) as it is called by paronomastic association between the terms Volga and "volk" (wolf). Andrei Zorin describes the setting of the novel in these terms: "in the second novel, the directly named Zaitil'shchina, or Zavolzh'e, serves only as a symbol for a lost corner of the earth. The specific topographical realities here are deliberately scarce, and the historical ones are so thoroughly mixed up that it is absolutely impossible to reconcile the events described with any particular part of our century. And this desire of the writer for the ultimate universalization of time and space in his novel finds its most vivid expression in the role played in his artistic world by the painting of Pieter Bruegel the Elder" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 252); "The theme of physical damage in the novel becomes another embodiment of the Zaitil'shchina, a land where nothing is being built, produced, and only occasionally repaired, and more often it decays, becomes unusable, breaks and steals" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 253). Vadim Kreid, titling his article "Zaitil'shchina," describes the "bezvremen'e" (the absence of time) as the "неизлечимая болезнь Заитильского бытия" (incurable illness of life in Zavol'zhe), while he also points out a specific "agnosticism" typical of this fictional world, based on "carelessness, inevitability of desolation, and nothingness (non-existence) as redemption" (беспечность, неизбежность опустошения и небытие как избавление) (216-217).
ru_trans: Название главы Ильи происходит от татарского названия реки Волга (Итиль) и напоминает о Задонщине, эпическом литературном тексте (датированным поздним 14-м веком) о Куликовской битве 1380 (его название происходит от названия реки Дон). Как "Задонщина раскрывает гуманность татарских войск и выражает искреннее сочувствие к горю, понятному и русским, и татарам" (Halperin, "The Golden Horde" 109), так и Затильщина описывает многообразный человеческий мир с помощью Волги (Заволжья) или Волчьей реки (Заволчье), обозначенный параносматической связью между словами "Волга" и "волк". А. Зорин описывает  обстановку романа так: "во втором романе, непосредственно названная Затильщина или Заволжье служит лишь символов затерянного уголка земли. Конкретные топографические реалии здесь нарочито скудны, а исторически так тщательно перемешаны, что совершенно невозможно соотнести описываемые события с каким0либо конкретным отрезком нашего века. И это стремление писателя к предельной универсализации времени и пространства в его романе находит свое наиболее яркое выражение в той роли, которую играет в его художественном мире картина Питера Брейгеля Старшего" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 252); "Тема физического ущерба в романе становится еще одним воплощением Затильщины, земли, где ничего не строится, не производится и лишь изредка ремонтируется, а чаще ветшает, приходит в негодность, ломается и крадется" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 253). В. Крейд, называя свою статью "Затильщиной", описывает "безвременье" (отсутствие времени) как "неизлечимая болезнь Затильского бытия", отмея при этом специфический "агностицизм, характерный этому вымышленному миру, основанном на "беспечности, неизбежности опустошения и небытии как избавлении" (216-217).

text: A variation on Krylobyl's name. Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227). According to Mario Caramitti, the character of Krylobyl is but an "hypostasis" of Drozhzhin, as he is here described dwelling by the [Volga](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB) ("Strategie" 131). Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by  the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).
ru_trans: Вариант имени Крылобыла. Крылобыл — ключевой персонаж, обитающий в мире мертвых (живет на другом берегу реки Итиль). Это неудивительно, учитывая, что имя у него говорящее: оно образовано из существительного "крыло" и глагола в прошедшем времени "был". Он — воплощение ангельского существа, направляющего Илью в его блужданиях, дающего ему идеи и помогающего ему в осмыслениях: в главе 14 именно Крылобыл предполагает происхождение буквы, и именно он описывается Ильёй как "умняга", который "учит", которому "он доверяет и кого он хвалит". В некотором смысле Крылобыль — Виргилий для Ильи или даже Беатриче в блужданиях Ильи по этим своеобразным Преисподней, Чистилищу и Раю. К концу романа его упомянет рассказчик в главе 16 (R275/E220), а в главе 17 Илья обратится к нему как к "Федоту Федорову" (R279/E227).

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivyan’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Another name given to Orina, the central female figure in the novel. In the chapters devoted to Yakov, she becomes his mother, thus the characters enact a variation on the Oedipal myth. Hanna Kolb writes: "She is a *Rossiia-mater'* (little mother Russia) (65) in eighteenth-century language [...] She is the Volga, the wolf-river which gives them crayfish to eat and water to drink, a stone under their heads, but also a stone around their necks. In each of the only two women's names that occur in the text, Orina and Mariia, may be heard "*rodina*" (native land), as well as "*mat'* (mother). Mariia is Iyakov's mother and the mother of God, about whom Il'a [sic] speaks in his Christmas sermon [...], both a mother goddess and the Mother of God. The lover Orina is raised in the figure of the Lady to sainthood, to the role of Blok's simultaneously life-giving [...] and death-giving "*neponiatnaia neznakomka*" (115)" (204). Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Ostanin (43) suggests interpretинг his last name as a variation of "Palamakherov" (from the verb palit', to burn), meaning someone who starts (or stops) fires. On that note, it would be worth recalling that final lines of the novel are, "So I dare you to burn, you dumb-as-a-bell, / My amazing, ingenious lines!" ("Попробуй пожги только, дурья башка, / Мои гениальные строчки") (R280/E230). Ostanin also observes that the name may find its origin in Gregory Palamas (in Russian, Palama), a Byzantine Greek theologian lived in the 14th century, known for his defense of hesychast spirituality.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

text: Colloquial: gimp, stump. See also Bruegel's painting *The Beggars* (1568): *Beggars* touches on a number of Sokolovian themes: deformities and handicaps, dancing, inversions of social order. It likewise features the fox imagery of *Between Dog and Wolf*. Manfred Sellink writes, “these paupers are performing (or rather trying to perform) a dance. The man in the centre, looking out at us, has straps with bells around his legs. The faces that can be seen have their mouths open, as it they are singing. The cripples are all dressed up, their white garments with foxtails mockingly evoking […] the expensive ermine robes worn by the most rich and powerful. This suggestion is strengthened by their equally evident headdresses, mimicking those on the heads of the mighty: a mitre, a crown and a fur cap. Given the fact that Bruegel is working here on a motif from his earlier Carnival painting, the painting touches on one of the essential aspects of Carnival festivities - a moment that briefly reverses the normal social order and class distinctions […] The appearance of the foxtails in conjunction with beggars in two totally different paintings, one dating from 1559 and the other from 1568, suggests that here the attribute is associated with popular customs, possibly connected with Carnival and Shrove Tuesday. There were longstanding traditions in which foxtails were seen as symbols of foolishness and deceit” (283).
ru_trans: Разговорное: калека, инвалид. См. также картину Брейгеля "Калеки" (1568). "Калеки" затрагивают ряд соколовских тем: уродство, калечество, танцы, инверсия социального порядка. В ней также присутствует образ лисы из "Между собакой и волком". М. Селлинк пишет: "Эти калеки исполняют (или, скорее, пытаются исполнить) танец. У человека в центре, смотрящего на нас, на ногах ремни с колокольчиками. Лица, которые можно увидеть, открывают рты, как будто они поют. Калеки все разодеты, их белые одежды с лисьими хвостами насмешливо вызывают в памяти […] дорогие горностаевые мантии, которые носят самые богатые и могущественные. Это предположение усиливается их столь же очевидными головными уборами, имитирующими те, что на головах могущественных людей: митра, корона и меховая шапка. Учитывая тот факт, что Брейгель работает здесь над мотивом из своей более ранней картины "Битва Масленицы и Поста", картина затрагивает один из существенных аспектов карнавальных празднеств — момент, который на короткое время меняет обычный социальный порядок и классовые различия […] Появление лисьих хвостов в сочетании с нищими на двух совершенно разных картинах, одна из которых датируется 1559 годом, а другая — 1568 годом, предполагает, что здесь этот атрибут связан с народными обычаями, возможно, связанными с Карнавалом и Масленицей. Существовали давние традиции, в которых лисьи хвосты рассматривались как символы глупости и обмана" (Sellink 283).

text: The title of Ilya's chapters in Russian, *Zaitil'shchina*, derives from the Tatar name of the Volga river (Itil'), and recalls the *[Zadonshchina](http://www.drevne.ru/lib/zadon_s.htm)*, an epic literary text (dated late 14th century) about the Battle of Kulikovo of 1380 (its title derives from the river Don). As "the Zadonshchina shows the humanity of the Tatar troops and expresses genuine sympathy for a grief the Russian and Tatar alike could understand” (Halperin, *The Golden Horde *109), the Zaitil'shchina describes the diverse human universe by the Volga (Zavol'zhe), or Wolf river (Zavol'che) as it is called by paronomastic association between the terms Volga and "volk" (wolf). Andrei Zorin describes the setting of the novel in these terms: "in the second novel, the directly named Zaitil'shchina, or Zavolzh'e, serves only as a symbol for a lost corner of the earth. The specific topographical realities here are deliberately scarce, and the historical ones are so thoroughly mixed up that it is absolutely impossible to reconcile the events described with any particular part of our century. And this desire of the writer for the ultimate universalization of time and space in his novel finds its most vivid expression in the role played in his artistic world by the painting of Pieter Bruegel the Elder" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 252); "The theme of physical damage in the novel becomes another embodiment of the Zaitil'shchina, a land where nothing is being built, produced, and only occasionally repaired, and more often it decays, becomes unusable, breaks and steals" ("Nasylaiushchii veter" 253). Vadim Kreid, titling his article "Zaitil'shchina," describes the "bezvremen'e" (the absence of time) as the "неизлечимая болезнь Заитильского бытия" (incurable illness of life in Zavol'zhe), while he also points out a specific "agnosticism" typical of this fictional world, based on "carelessness, inevitability of desolation, and nothingness (non-existence) as redemption" (беспечность, неизбежность опустошения и небытие как избавление) (216-217).

text: Braid, scythe, or sandback/spit. The ambiguity of the word “kosa” has a famous literary “predecessor” in Aleksandr Blok’s drama *Balaganchik* (*The Puppet Show*, 1906). The female character of Columbine has a “kosa” behind her back: either a hair braid or a scythe. The “mystics” warn Pierrot about her being Death, but he calls her his bride (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”; I don't listen to fairy tales. I am a simple man. You will not deceive me. This is Columbine. This is my bride). The ambiguity is also stressed by the character of the Author who enters the scene and exclaims: “Я не признаю [...] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” (I do not recognize [...] such allegorical wordplay: it is indecent to call a woman's braid a scythe of death! It denigrates a lady's status!). In the end, Pierrot sadly discovers that this Columbine was just a “cardboard bride” (Она картонной невестой была). The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). Read the original by Blok [here](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B8%D0%BA_(%D0%91%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%BA)).

У героини по имени Колумбина есть "коса" за спиной: это или плетеные волосы, или же серп. "Мистики" предупреждают Пьера о том, что Колумбина есть Смерть, но от отрицает это, называя её свой невестой (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”). Неоднозначность усиливается, когда герой Автора вторгается в сцену и восклицает: Я не признаю […] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” В конце Пьер с горестью обнаруживает, что всё это время Колубмина была "картонной невестой". Ключевая тема, связывающая женскую любовь со смертью, проводит параллель между соколовским романом и блоковским "Балаганчиком", хоть она и разрабатывалась продолжительной литературной традицией в течение очень долгого времени (например, Эрос и Танатос, "Ненавижу и люблю" Катулла). text: Another name given to Orina, the central female figure in the novel. In the chapters devoted to Yakov, she becomes his mother, thus the characters enact a variation on the Oedipal myth. Hanna Kolb writes: "She is a *Rossiia-mater*' (little mother Russia) (65) in eighteenth-century language […] She is the Volga, the wolf-river which gives them crayfish to eat and water to drink, a stone under their heads, but also a stone around their necks. In each of the only two women's names that occur in the text, Orina and Mariia, may be heard "*rodina*" (native land), as well as "*mat*'" (mother). Mariia is Iyakov's mother and the mother of God, about whom Il'a [sic] speaks in his Christmas sermon […], both a mother goddess and the Mother of God. The lover Orina is raised in the figure of the Lady to sainthood, to the role of Blok's simultaneously life-giving […] and death-giving "*neponiatnaia neznakomka*" (115)" (204). Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. [от Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: Throughout the novel, Yakov's identity has come into question. In chapter 5, he is associated with the idea of camouflage. He may or may not be Ilya's son with Orina. Furthermore, he may be the author of every part of the novel. In short, much like Yakov himself, the reader struggles to sort out his character as well. These questions that blend identity, time, and personhood are typical of Sokolov's three novels. Larissa Rudova writes of *Palisandriia*'s hero: "Since no true historical experience is possible, Palisandr is bogged down with the existential question about who he is" ("Paradigms" 68).

Более того, он может быть автором каждой главы романа. Одним словом, так же, как и сам Яков, не может разобраться в его персонаже. Эти вопросы, размывающие идентичность, время и личность, типичны для трех романов Соколова. Set expression: ain't that stupid, wasn't born yesterday. Sokolov explains: "The expression [...] means: an adult, an independent, altogether reasonable person, For example, an older brother offers help to a younger one in solving some task, and he answers: 'Thank you, no need, I have a mustache myself,' that is, I can handle it myself, I am already an adult. The expression is humorous precisely because of the truncation of the mustache. Here, as often happens in established expressions, grammatical correctness has fallen victim to rhyme. Or thus: rhyme has defeated the grammatical norm. In this line, this saying is used in a self-ironic sense: the poet—perhaps he has a mustache, but not necessarily—thanks to another flash of lightning, when he sees his reflection in the cat's eye, he grins at his dubious importance. You can translate this expression in prose like this: 'The cat in the eye is none other than me, in the flesh'" (personal correspondence, August 4, 2023).
ru_trans: Устойчивое выражение: не вчера родился. Соколов объясняет: "Выражение ‘сам с усам‘, то есть ‘с усами‘, означает ‘взрослый, самостоятельный, достаточно разумный человек‘. Например, старший брат предлагает младшему помощь в решении какой-то задачи, а тот отвечает: ‘Спасибо, не надо, я сам с усам‘; то есть, ‘сам справлюсь, я уже взрослый‘. Выражение несет юмористический характер именно благодаря усечению усов. Здесь, как это нередко случается в устоявшихся выражениях, грамматическая правильность пала жертвой рифмы. Или так: рифма победила грамматическую норму. В данной строке эта поговорка использована в самоироническом смысле: поэт — возможно, он при усах, но необязательно, — благодаря очередной вспышке молнии увидев свое отражение в глазу кота, усмехается над своей сомнительной важностью. Перевести это выражение прозой можно так: ‘У кота в глазу — не кто иной, как я собственной персоной’" (личная переписка, 4 августа 2023).

text: According to Boguslawski's annotations, *zimar'* refers to Andrei Voznesensky's poem "Song-travesty from the spectacle 'Antiworlds'" (1963) ("Annotations" 233). It combines the word *zima* (winter) with the ending of *ianvar'* (January) to refer to the winter time. Perhaps a reference to the Orion constellation visible during the winter solstice. According to the mythology, Orion fell in love with Merope (along with many other women) and raped her, similar to the story told here by Orina. Constellation-heavens motif.
ru_trans: Согласно аннотациям Богуславского, "зимарь" — отсылка на стихотворение Андрея Вознесенского "Песенка-травести из спектакля Антимиры" (1963) ("Annotations" 233). Образовано сочетанием слов "зима" и "январь", подразумевая на зимнее время. Возможно, также намек на созвездие Ориона, видимое на небе в период зимнего солнцестояния. Согласно мифологии, Орион полюбил Меропу (как и многих других женщин) и насильно овладел ею, что напоминает историю Орины. Мотив созвездий-неба.

1. A person with a physical disability or leg injury. Ilya has lost a leg.
2. Twisted silk, worsted, or cotton with cord or wire running through it, used chiefly as upholstery trimming. Word play on "wool over my eyes."

See also Bruegel's painting *The Beggars* (1568): *Beggars *touches on a number of Sokolovian themes: deformities and handicaps, dancing, inversions of social order. It likewise features the fox imagery of *Between Dog and Wolf*. Manfred Sellink writes, “these paupers are performing (or rather trying to perform) a dance. The man in the centre, looking out at us, has straps with bells around his legs. The faces that can be seen have their mouths open, as it they are singing. The cripples are all dressed up, their white garments with foxtails mockingly evoking […] the expensive ermine robes worn by the most rich and powerful. This suggestion is strengthened by their equally evident headdresses, mimicking those on the heads of the mighty: a mitre, a crown and a fur cap. Given the fact that Bruegel is working here on a motif from his earlier Carnival painting, the painting touches on one of the essential aspects of Carnival festivities - a moment that briefly reverses the normal social order and class distinctions […] The appearance of the foxtails in conjunction with beggars in two totally different paintings, one dating from 1559 and the other from 1568, suggests that here the attribute is associated with popular customs, possibly connected with Carnival and Shrove Tuesday. There were longstanding traditions in which foxtails were seen as symbols of foolishness and deceit” (283).

text: Коса (*kosa*) in Russian: braid, scythe, or sandback/spit. The ambiguity of the word “kosa” has a famous literary “predecessor” in Aleksandr Blok’s drama *Balaganchik* (*The Puppet Show*, 1906). The female character of Columbine has a “kosa” behind her back: either a hair braid or a scythe. The “mystics” warn Pierrot about her being Death, but he calls her his bride (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”; I don't listen to fairy tales. I am a simple man. You will not deceive me. This is Columbine. This is my bride). The ambiguity is also stressed by the character of the Author who enters the scene and exclaims: “I do not recognize [...] such allegorical wordplay: it is indecent to call a woman's braid a scythe of death! It denigrates a lady's status!" In the end, Pierrot sadly discovers that this Columbine was just a “cardboard bride." The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). text: Set expression: ain't that stupid, wasn't born yesterday. Sokolov explains: "The expression [...] means: an adult, an independent, altogether reasonable person, For example, an older brother offers help to a younger one in solving some task, and he answers: 'Thank you, no need, I have a mustache myself,' that is, I can handle it myself, I am already an adult. The expression is humorous precisely because of the truncation of the mustache. Here, as often happens in established expressions, grammatical correctness has fallen victim to rhyme. Or thus: rhyme has defeated the grammatical norm. In this line, this saying is used in a self-ironic sense: the poet—perhaps he has a mustache, but not necessarily—thanks to another flash of lightning, when he sees his reflection in the cat's eye, he grins at his dubious importance. You can translate this expression in prose like this: 'The cat in the eye is none other than me, in the flesh'" (personal correspondence, August 4, 2023).

text: D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. [от Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).
ru_trans: Крылобыл — ключевой персонаж, обитающий в мире мертвых (живущий на другом берегу Итиля, в Выдогоще). Это неудивительно, ведь его "говорящее имя" образовано словами "крыло" и "был". Он — ипостась ангельского существа, направляющего Илью в его странствиях и наводящего его на идеи и размышления: в главе 4 именно Крылобыл выдвинул мысль о происхождении буквы "ж"; именно Крылобыла в 14 главе Илья описывает как "умнягу", который "увещает", " кому доверяю, кого хвалю". В каком-то смысле Крылобыл — это Вергилий или даже Беатриче Ильи в его странствованиях по этому особого рода Аду, Чистилищу и Раю. Ближе к концу романа рассказчик в главе 16 (R275/E220) и Илья в главе 17 будут обращаться к нему как "Федот Федоров" (R279/E227).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Like the prints in the snow that fade away, so, too, do the things left behind by peoples and cultures. This is the opposite of Pushkin's message in his famous 1836 poem "Exegi Monumentum." Read it in the original and in an English translation [here](https://ruverses.com/alexander-pushkin/exegi-monumentum/1945/). Indeed, Yakov's apparent invitation to burn his verses will similarly be reversed at the end of the Note. Sokolov responds: "As a keep Soviet critic would write, Pushkin's verse is life-affirming, while Sokolov's, on the contrary, is decadent" (personal communication, August 4, 2023).

text: English: honeymoon. Flowers in the flowerbed mentioned just before. Ostanin suggests that here it refers to tulips, lilies, or Chinese roses (92). However, it is likely a misspelling or play on  "anemone" (commonly called wildflowers). Since they are "anemic," they are white. According to Sokolov, these flowers are "a variety of fringed tulips, matured ones are half a meter high, but the young sprouts are, of course, small. Anemic means pale, weak, feeble" (personal communication, July 29, 2023). Plant motif.
ru_trans: В английском языке: honeymoon, медовый месяц. Цветы на клумбе, упомянутой ранее. Останин предполагает, что здесь речь идет о тюльпанах, лилиях или китайских розах (92). text: Numerous characters in the novel, and in Sokolov's work in general, suffer from disabilities.

Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: This name calls to mind two famous poetic "albatrosses": Baudelaire's (read it [here](https://fleursdumal.org/poem/200)) and Coleridge's from *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* (read it [here](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43997/the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner-text-of-1834)). Addressing the latter subtext's image of a bird wrapped around a sailor's neck in penance, José Vergara writes, "Albatrosov is an embodiment of Ilya’s perceived betrayal by Orina, who it is said, sleeps with a number of sailors under the aforementioned overturned boat on the banks of the Volga, as well as guilt over his own actions. Ilya takes on his sorrow when he meets Albatrosov on a train after his separation from Orina. The avian-sailor thus serves to remind Ilya of the past he cannot escape. […] The anthropomorphized bird imagery, in this way, underscores Ilya’s lingering psychological trauma, both that which he himself caused and that which he received" ("Flap" 372). Animal-human motif. In a 2004 interview with Mario Caramitti, Sokolov comments on the suggestion of art predicting life in mysterious ways mentioning this specific character: “In the winter of 1978 I was living in Michigan and working on my second novel. One of the characters in the book, named Al'batrosov, has a background as a stoker on a ship. I was outlining the character by modeling him on my half-brother, a sailor, who was aboard a freighter at the time. Without thinking about the possible consequences, I made Albatrosov's fate take a turn for the worse: an explosion in the engine room takes off his arm. When the book came out, I learned that in the same days that I was writing that episode my brother lost an arm to an accident. This is, I would say, the cruelest and most disconcerting example in my practice as a writer. But on the whole what I write often comes true. More often, unfortunately, than I would like, since I generally write about unpleasant things” (“Sokolov, il fabbro pellegrino della prosa russa” 12). The same concept is described by the author in his 1981 essay *On Secret Tablets*: “things described in fiction come true; fate suggests to the neglected in spirit solutions that it has already found. And it does not make any difference whether the master creates life myths or they create him: the text has been recorded in the same place, on secret tablets. And nothing else but fate will answer all the questions and decide what will remain – silence or the word. And, if necessary, it’ll rip out our sinful tongues” (7).

Данная фамилия наводит на мысль о двух знаменитых поэтических "альбатросах": бодлеровском (читать [здесь](https://fleursdumal.org/poem/200)) и кольриджском из "Сказания о старом мореходе" (читать [здесь](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43997/the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner-text-of-1834)). Обращаясь к дальнейшему образу птицы, обвевающей шею маяка в знак покаяния, Х. Вергара пишет: "Альбатросов — воплощение осознаваемого Ильей предательства Орины, которая, согласно слухам, спит с несколькими моряками под вышеупомянутой перевернутой лодкой на берегу Волги; а также чувства вины за собственные поступки. Илья перенимает на себя горе Альбатросова, когда встречает его в поезде после разлуки с Ориной. Так, птица-моряк напоминает Илье о прошлом, от которого он не может убежать. [...] Антропоморфные образы птиц, таким образом, подчеркивают затянувшуюся травму Ильи — как ту, которую он нанес себе сам, так и ту, которую он получил" ("Flap" 372). Мотив животных-людей.  
В 2004 году Соколов упомянул этого персонажа в интервью с Марио Карамитти, комментируя предположение о том, что искусство неким таинственным образом предсказывает жизнь: "Зимой 1987 года я проживал в Мичигане и работал над моим вторым романом. Персонаж по фамилии Альбатросов работал кочегаром на корабле. Я набросал его по подобию моего сводного брата, моряка, который в то время служил на грузовом судне. Не думая о возможных последствиях, я склонил судьбу Альбатросова к наихудшему: взрывом в машинном отделении ему оторвало руку. Когда книга вышла в свет, я узнал, что в тот же самый день когда я писал эту сцену, мой брат потерял руку в результате несчастного случая. Это, я бы сказал, самый жестокий и обескураживающий пример из моей писательской практики. В целом, многое из того, что я пишу, оказывается правдой. К сожалению, чаще, чем мне бы хотелось, так как я в основном пишу о неприятных вещах" (“Sokolov, il fabbro pellegrino della prosa russa” 12).  Ту же идею он описал в эссе "На сокровенных скрижалях" (1981): "написанное сбывается. Ибо судьба подсказывает беспризорному духом решения, которые уже приняла. И мастер ли сочиняет житейские мифы, они ли — его, все равно: текст промыслен все там же, на сокровенных скрижалях. И не судьба ли ответит на все вопросы, не она ли решит, что пребудет: молчание или слово? И если потребуется — вырвет наши грешные языки" (7).

Alexander Boguslawski writes: "Hence the sexual act [in Sokolov's novel] is not only a happy union, but a bitter struggle; a fleeting moment of bliss and ecstasy ultimately ends in misery and suffering. Perhaps these thoughts may be explained as a distant reflection of the Freudian conflict between life instinct—Eros and death instinct—Thanatos (or even a merger between sex drive and death drive)" ("Death" 239–240). text: This verb both introduces the bird motif, associating characters with birds (and, more generally, animals), and suggests via its figurative meaning ("being forced to be somewhere") the itinerant nature of Ilya. José Vergara suggests that Sokolov's bird imagery "underscores the inherent tie between the characters (humanity) and nature in the novel. That is, the natural world in the guise of various animals does not only reflect the characters’ emotions and experiences. They may wish to overcome their status as beings of flesh, blood, and nature, but the bird imagery – among other things – constantly reminds them of their earthbound existence. They seek to escape the pull of the mundane and wearisome existence they live and to reach an ideal, but they are consistently dragged back down" ("Flap" 364).
ru_trans: Данный глагол и вводит "птичий мотив", связывающую персонажей и птицами (или вообще животными), и образно подсказывает передвижной и странствующий характер Ильи. Хосе Вергара считает, что птичья тематика Соколова "подчеркивает присущую роману связь между персонажами (человечеством) и природой". То есть мир природы в облике различных животных не только отражает эмоции и переживания персонажей. Они могут хотеть преодолеть свой статус существ из плоти, крови и природы, но образы птиц - помимо всего прочего - постоянно напоминают им об их земном существовании. Они стремятся освободиться от притяжения обыденного и утомительного существования, которым они живут, и достичь идеала, но их постоянно тянет обратно вниз" ("Flap" 364).

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он — юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: Another instance of humans transforming into animals. Ostanin also notes a connection to *A School for Fools*, namely the scene in which the hero visits his grandmother's grave: "a multicolored winter butterfly that was sitting on the branch of the elder gets scared and flies in the direction of the next grave; the angel only shudders but does not fly away; he stays with grandmother" (*Shkola* R78/E95). In general, the link between butterflies (or moths) and death is stressed both in *A School for Fools* and in this novel. Indeed, butterflies are often mentioned in relation to the idea of a short (but bright, beautiful, and light) life. Animal-human motif.

text: Made of oak. Mikhail Epstein notes that in Russian poetry “the oak tree is separated from the other trees, which makes it the king of the tree kingdom. It embodies the highest degree of hardness, courage, strength and majesty. It is this clarity of the original meaning that made the image of the oak tree especially popular in the early stages of poetry, and then weakened its significance when the imagery of poetry began to become more complex and overcome the unambiguity of folklore and allegorical musings. […] The oak tree in Russian poetry, as well as in world folklore, symbolizes the power of life that overcame death; that is why the decay of the oak tree acts as an ominous sign of the collapse of life, the invasion of demonic forces in its sanctuary” (47, 50). Plant motif.

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Ilya returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."
ru_trans: В письме от 24 февраля 1981 года Д. Бартон Джонсон спросил Соколова: "Не могли бы Вы прокомментировать структуру 'Картинок'? Они все задуманы как живописные грезы будущего художника, пока он (Яков?) глядит в окно из школьного окна?" В своем ответе от 3 марта 1981 года Соколов объясняет, как в "алкогольном воображении неудачливого художника и поэта-графомана" Якова пейзаж и человеческие и нечеловеческие фигуры брейгелевских "Охотников на снегу" накладываются на то, что он наблюдает вокруг себя: "Яков представляет себе (в плане мечт или, вернее, дневных грез) все свои картины, которые он мог бы написать, и как будто бы 'Охотники на снегу' — одна из картин его авторства. Однако в Записке под названием 'К незнакомому живописцу' (думаю, так; книги у меня с собой нет — я ее одолжил) поэт Яков критикует Брейгеля, которого он не знает, за неточность изображения Городнища и одежд охотников (и так далее)." Соколов поясняет, что для Якова вся его жизнь — "дневные грезы", и что картины в его воображении смешиваются, будто бы "в калейдоскопе" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).

text: Ostanin (43) suggests to interpret his last name as a variation of "Palamakherov" (from the verb palit', to burn), meaning someone who starts (or stops) fires. On that note, it would be worth recalling that final lines of the novel are "So I dare you to burn, you dumb-as-a-bell, / My amazing, ingenious lines!" ("Попробуй пожги только, дурья башка, / Мои гениальные строчки") (R280/E230). Ostanin also observes that the name may find its origin in Gregory Palamas (in Russian, Palama), a Byzantine Greek theologian lived in the 14th century, known for his defense of hesychast spirituality.
ru_trans: Останин предлагает интерпретировать эту фамилию как вариацию "Паломахеров" (от глагола "палить"), что характеризует разжигающего (или тушащего) огонь человека. На этой ноте, стоит вспомнить завершающие строки романа: "Попробуй пожги только, дурья башка, / Мои гениальные строчки" (R280/E230). Останин также замечает, что фамилия, возможно, берет начало от Григория Паламы, греческого православного богослова XIV века, известного обоснованием духовной практики исихаизма (Ostanin 43).

text: According to Orthodox tradition, among others, the ninth day after death is crucial, as it is on this day that the soul learns whether it will be accepted into Heaven. For that reason, the wake is traditionally held nine days after a person's death. Bygodozhd' could here represent the "city of death" or something similar (since when they leave for Bygodozhd', people will drink, cry in their name on the ninth day, and so on).
ru_trans: Согласно православной традиции, в то числе, девятый день после смерти имеет особое значение, ведь на этот день душа получает ответ, примут ли ее на небеса. Поэтому поминки обычно длятся девять дней после смерти человека. Быгодождь здесь символизирует "город смерти" и что-то подобное (ведь когда они отправляются в Быгодождь, люди пьют, льют слезы в их имя и т. д.).
