text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он - юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Ilya returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."
ru_trans: Отчество Якова Алфеева намекает на то, что его отец — Илья. Однако данная интерпретация представляется спорной. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает: "Яков — сын Ильи: в такой же степени, как и всё в сумеречном мире меж собакой и волком. Тем не менее, и Яков, и Илья не имеют ни малейшего подозрения об этом, и когда их дальнейшие жизни в качестве точильщика и собаковода окончательно и бесповортно пересекаются, они в равной степени и не знают о своей скоротечной дружбе в больнице (…). [Яков] воссоздает образ хромого Эдипа. Он невольно убивает и отца, и (хоть и не буквально) "женится" на копии своей матери. Соколов переосмыслил и инсценировал греческую трагедию об Эдипе в верховьях Волги" (“Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212).  Действительно, Илья будет убит Яковым в качестве отомщения за то, что первый (в сумерках, пересекая замороженную реку) ошибочно принимает одну из собак последнего за волка и убивает ее. После того, как охотник крадет его костыли, Илья возвращается, чтобы убить собак. Для более подробного ознакомления с мифопоэтикой Соколова см. работу И. В. Ащеуловой "Творчество Саши Соколова в контексте литературного процесса 60–80-х".

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах ("Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Diminutive form of Orina. Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Уменьшительная форма имени "Орина". Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: As often happens in the novel (since its very title), phraseologisms and metaphors are both taken as such, and as sentences referring to concrete, real phenomena. Elena Kravchenko argues that "Sokolov's texts are not a denial of the real, but an acknowledgement of its insufficiency. Both *School for Fools* and *Between Dog and Wolf* speak about how the world contains barely anything of what we value in it. [...] Working within a complex network of reflections, Sokolov offers reality his (writing) hand. For, in order for it to become a meaningful event, reality requires mediation" (*The Prose* 130).
ru_trans: Как это нередко встречается в романе (начиная с заглавия), фразеологизмы и метафоры принимают буквальное значение и относятся к реальным событиям. Е. Кравченко утверждает: "Тексты Соколова не отрицают реальность, а скорее признают ее неполноценность. Как в "Школе для дураков", так и в "Между собакой и волком" говорится о том, как мало в мире есть того, что мы ценим. [...] Работая со сложной системой отражений, Соколов предлагает реальность свою (писательскую) руку помощи. Ведь для того, чтобы реальность приобрела смысл, ей необходимен посредник" (Kravchenko, "The Prose" 130).

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in this chapter who Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise." In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Typically only used in the negative: невтерпеж (low: to be unbearable). So, here: bearable. Alexander Boguslawski notes that variations on this word are used in four key moments in the novel (R155, 157, 225, 254/E12, 14–15, 132, 185) and that the "close parallels between the first and last use of the phrase should be noted — this is the frame within which two other versions of the expression exist. These two framing elements are built around the word *nevterpezh*, a colloquial adverb, usually used after a noun or pronoun in dative case and often with auxiliary verbs to be or to become. Thus, the expression "mne stalo nevterpezh" [it became unbearable to me; I could not stand it any longer], [sic] is common. However, Sokolov makes some important alterations to the expression — first, he discards the dative government and substitutes another verb for the auxiliary" ("How Sokolov's" 218).
ru_trans: Обычно используется как негативное утверждение "невтерпеж" (просторечное: невыносимо). Здесь же: выносимо. А. Богуславский отмечает, что вариации этого слова используются в четырех ключевых сценах романа (R155, 157, 225, 254/E12, 14–15, 132, 185) и что "что следует отметить тесную связь между первым и последним употреблениями слова — они служат как рамка, внутри которой существуют остальные два выражения. Эта окантовка выстраивается вокруг слова 'невтерпеж', разговорном наречии, обычно используемом после существительного или местоимения в дательном падеже, зачастую с вспомогательными глаголами 'быть' или 'стать'. Так, выражение 'мне стало невтерпеж' широко распространенно. Однако Соколов вносит в это выражение несколько примечательных изменений: прежде всего, он отбрасывает дательный падеж и заменяет один вспомогательный глагол другим" ("How Sokolov's" 218).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен (*paklen*) and неклен (*neklen*) are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Neklina, Paklina). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Krylobyl participated in Ilya's drowning after the latter killed Yakov's dogs. A reference to the Last Judgment — according to Christian faith, the time when Jesus will return and judge all souls to determine whether they will reside in Heaven or Hell. See [Matthew 6:9–13](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+6%3A9-13&version=ESV;NRT) and [Matthew 25:31-46](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2025%3A31-46&version=ESV,NRT). Johnson writes of Sokolov's time as a game warden on the Upper Volga: "Sokolov's predecessor, whose cabin and effects he had inherited, had come to a bad end. There had been an incident involving the hunting dogs of a neighbor. A feud ensued, and the game garden had been found drowned. The official investigation had yielded little but suspicions" ("Sasha Sokolov: A Literary Biography" 208).

[От Матфея 6:9-13](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+6%3A9-13&version=ESV;NRT) и [От Матфея 25:31-46](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2025%3A31-46&version=NIV,NRT). text: Ostanin identifies this as an allusion to Mikhail Lermontov's 1837 poem "Borodino": "Что ж мы? на зимние квартиры?" (35). Read the poem and an English translation [here](https://ruverses.com/mikhail-lermontov/borodino/1830/). Responding to a question regarding similarities between his style and that of Vladimir Nabokov, Sokolov said, "I've surmized that a similarity in our styles might come from a common source: We share favorite writers. It may be enough to point to Gogol' and Lermontov. By connecting these two, a system of coordinates appears, from which one can determine style. Of course, only if both writers are favorites" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 353). For more on Sokolov and Nabokov, see D. Barton Johnson's "Saša Sokolov and Vladimir Nabokov." There, the critic writes, "After arriving in Vienna in October 1975, Sokolov read (in Russian) *Lolita* and *The Gift* and was surprised to note similarities between the avant-garde prose style of *Škola dlja durakov* and Nabokov's prose techniques [...] Dismayed, Sokolov determined to develop a new, distinctive voice, one not under the shadow of the older writer. This search led to the exotic language of his 1980 *Meždu sobakoj i volkom*" (154). Evgeny Sokolov calls *Between Dog and Wolf* a "poema squared," riffing on Gogol's characterization of his novel *Dead Souls* as a poema (10).
ru_trans: Останин определяет это как ссылку на на стихотворение М. Лермонтова "Бородино": "Что ж мы? на зимние квартиры?" (35). Прочитать оригинал и английский перевод стихотворения можно [здесь](https://ruverses.com/mikhail-lermontov/borodino/1830/). Отвечая на вопрос о схожести его стиля с набоковским, Соколов сказал: "Я предполагаю, что схожесть наших стилей объясняется общим источником: мы делим любимых писателей. Достаточно хотя бы отметить Гоголя и Лермонтова. Их соединение приводит к образованию системы координат, из которой можно определить стиль. Конечно же, такое возможно только если оба писателя любимые" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 353). Больше о Соколове и Набокове можно прочитать у Д. Бартона Джонсона "Саша Соколов и Владимир Набоков". Там критик пишет: "После переезда в Вену в октябре 1975 года Соколов прочитал (на русском) "Лолиту" и "Дар" и с удивлением отметил схожесть авангардного стиля прозы *Школы для дураков* и техники набоковской прозы. […] Обескураженный, Соколов решил выработать новый, самобытный голос, не прячущийся в тени старшего писателя. Этот поиск привел к экзотическому стилю его романа 1980 года "Между собакой и волком"" (D. Barton Johnson's "Saša Sokolov and Vladimir Nabokov", 154). Евгений Соколов называет "Между собакой и волком" "поэмой в квадрате", что напоминает характеризацию Гоголем своего романа "Мертвые души" как поэму (Evgeny Sokolov 10).

text:
Gury's first appearance. Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*.
Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14).
Animal motif.

text:
Sokolov explains: "In the years we are talking about, many houses were not, pardon the expression, gasified, and in many kitchens people cooked on kerosene stoves, AKA kerosinki, which made those kitchens and the adjoining premises smell of kerosene fumes. This smell is nostalgic to me: it brings back memories of that unpretentious, poor, but in its own way cozy life of communal houses and dachas of the forties and fifties.
At that time and later in the city courtyards in the evenings there was an interesting life: neighbors played soccer, dominoes, cards, sang guitar songs, drank hot drinks, discussed news and gossiped. An individual walking through the courtyard became an object of attention, a familiar person was greeted, an unfamiliar one was silently looked at to discuss who he was, how he was dressed and where he was going. In general, the courtyard community was interested in every passerby, noticed and met everyone in one way or another. They would meet them if the weather was good. In this case, the weather is bad - damp, slushy, probably windy, and the barracks, i.e. the population, the people of the barracks, will not meet the jubilant centipede, because the courtyard is empty, everyone is at home, no one wants to catch a cold, get polyps in the nose or inflammation of the glands. I did not use this term, I used a colloquial variant, usually this problem is interpreted simply: he had, let's say, tonsils, i.e. inflammation of the tonsils. Or a case like this: the medical report says 'he died of a myocardial infarction', but the neighbors say: 'of heart'. I dare to explain why fragments of bottle glass do not shine either at the pier or in garbage heaps: a certain critic [admired](https://proza.ru/2013/10/12/967?ysclid=lkq42bv7s5481764198) Chekhov's ability to describe natural phenomena and landscapes very laconically and gave an example: in a certain story Chekhov, to make it clear that the night is moonlit, offers one detail: a fragment of bottle glass shines near the pier" (personal communication, July 29, 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "В годы, о коих речь, многие дома не были, простите за выражение, газифицированы, и на многих кухнях готовили на керосиновых плитках, АКА керосинки, отчего на тех кухнях и в примыкающих к ним помещениях пахло керосиновой гарью. Этот запах мне ностальгичен: он навевает воспоминания о том неказистом, бедном, но по-своему уютном быте коммуналок и дач сороковых и пятидесятых. В то время и позже в городских дворах по вечерам имела место интересная жизнь: соседи играли в футбол, в домино, в карты, пели песни под гитару, распивали горячительные напитки, обсуждали новости и плели сплетни. Идущий через двор индивид становился объектом внимания, знакомого приветствовали, незнакомого молча рассматривали, чтобы потом обсудить, кто он такой, как одет и куда идет. Вобщем, дворовое сообщество всяким прохожим интересовалось, всякого в той или иной мере замечало, встречало. Встречало, если была хорошая погода. В данном случае погода плохая - сыро, слякотно, вероятно, дует, и бараки, читай - население, люди бараков - не встретят ликующую сороконожку, ибо двор пуст, все сидят дома, никто не хочет простыть, получить полипы в носу или воспаление гланд. Я этот термин не использовал, употребил разговорный вариант,  обычно об этой проблеме толкуют просто: у него, мол гланды, то есть воспаление оных. Или такой случай: в эпикризе написано: умер от инфаркта миокарда, а соседи говорят: от сердца. Осмелюсь пояснить, отчего осколки бутылочного стекла не блестят ни у пристани, ни в мусорных кучах: некий критик [восхищался](https://proza.ru/2013/10/12/967?ysclid=lkq42bv7s5481764198) умением Чехова описывать природные явления и пейзажи весьма лаконично и привел пример: в каком-то рассказе Чехов, чтобы дать понять, что ночь лунная, предлагает одну деталь: возле пристани блестит осколок бутылочного стекла" (личная переписка, 29 июля 2023).

text: Leader of an uprising of Volga Cossacks and peasants in the second half of the seventeenth century that shook the Muscovite government of Aleksei I in the southeast. His victorious march came to an end in the autumn of 1670. Troops armed according to the Western standard liberated the besieged town of Simbirsk (now known as [Ulyanovsk](https://www.google.com/maps/place/simbirsk/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x415d365f8f42b3f5:0x2152ff0847091be4?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwj4x9uvgun_AhWcFFkFHb1BBOkQ8gF6BAgREAA&ved=2ahUKEwj4x9uvgun_AhWcFFkFHb1BBOkQ8gF6BAgWEAE))  from rebels in October. A tremendous famine in 1670–71 led to the revolt’s collapse. In the spring of 1671, Razin fell prisoner; he was later sentenced to death and executed on September 24 in Moscow. The memory of the revolt and of Stepan (Sten'ka) Razin remained alive in folk songs. Also known as Stenka Razin.

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. [...] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). Animal motif.
ru_trans: Гурий — один из охотников, живущих у реки. Его смерть детально описана в главе 14: во время ледяной гонки "начал Гурий за пару верст до поворота понаддавать, а доезжачий — поотставать, но принял Гурий немного правее, чем следовало, и угодил в полынью, в промоину в районе фарватера. <…> и течением его сразу под лед сволокло". Так как до наступления весны достать его тело невозможно, его похороны были устроены "без его фактического присутствия" (R260/E196). Краткое упоминание этого эпизода уже было в главе 1: "вот кто обожал пошаркать и раскатиться по гладкому на точеных, которые и стали причиной того, что мы клиента утратили, а погребальщики клиента же обрели" (R150/E3). Еврейское имя, означает "маленький лев" (gur 'aryeh). Возможно, есть связь с "Аллегорией благоразумия" Тициана. Останин предполагает отсылку к Гурию Казанскому (ок. 1500-1563) (Ostanin 14). text: Oak. Mikhail Epstein notes that in Russian poetry “the oak tree is separated from the other trees, which makes it the king of the tree kingdom. It embodies the highest degree of hardness, courage, strength and majesty. It is this clarity of the original meaning that made the image of the oak tree especially popular in the early stages of poetry, and then weakened its significance when the imagery of poetry began to become more complex and overcome the unambiguity of folklore and allegorical musings. […] The oak tree in Russian poetry, as well as in world folklore, symbolizes the power of life that overcame death; that is why the decay of the oak tree acts as an ominous sign of the collapse of life, the invasion of demonic forces in its sanctuary” (47, 50). Plant motif.

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Отчество Якова Алфеева намекает на то, что его отец — Илья. Однако данная интерпретация представляется спорной. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает: "Яков — сын Ильи: в такой же степени, как и всё в сумеречном мире меж собакой и волком. Тем не менее, и Яков, и Илья не имеют ни малейшего подозрения об этом, и когда их дальнейшие жизни в качестве точильщика и собаковода окончательно и бесповортно пересекаются, они в равной степени и не знают о своей скоротечной дружбе в больнице (…). [Яков] воссоздает образ хромого Эдипа. Он невольно убивает и отца, и (хоть и не буквально) "женится" на копии своей матери. Соколов переосмыслил и инсценировал греческую трагедию об Эдипе в верховьях Волги" (“Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212).  Действительно, Илья будет убит Яковым в качестве отомщения за то, что первый (в сумерках, пересекая замороженную реку) ошибочно принимает одну из собак последнего за волка и убивает ее. После того, как охотник крадет его костыли, Илья возвращается, чтобы убить собак. Для более подробного ознакомления с мифопоэтикой Соколова см. работу И. В. Ащеуловой "Творчество Саши Соколова в контексте литературного процесса 60–80-х".

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Ilya returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Boris Ostanin also notes that in the Koran the hoopoe turns up late to King Solomon's congress of birds but manages to escape the death sentence after he explains that he was spying in Queen Sheba's kingdom; Solomon then sends the hoopoe with a message to Sheba (39). In this way, additional links between the myth and Ilya are activated: Ilya's letter to Pozhilykh sent after his own murder at the hands of Yakov, mail, an escape from death (Vergara, "Flap" 367). Animal-human motif.

text: The mythical Firebird from Slavic folklore. Read the original [here](https://xn----7sbb5adknde1cb0dyd.xn--p1ai/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/) and an English translation [here](http://www.artrusse.ca/fairytales/firebird.htm). The story is set in a kingdom where an unknown thief is stealing apples from the king’s garden. The three princes must find out who is the thief: the younger, Ivan, observes that it is a marvelous Firebird stealing the apples, but he is only able to catch one of the bird’s feathers. The king is amazed by its beauty and orders his sons to capture the Firebird, an adventure that will be successful in the end only for Ivan. However, on his way back, he takes a rest and his brothers, out of envy, decide to kill him. Thanks to the help of a wolf friend, Ivan manages to recover and reestablish order in the kingdom. The motif of theft and the figure of the wolf (in the folk tale, a positive hero according to Vladimir Propp, famed Soviet folklorist) are relevant to Sokolov’s novel, too. The Firebird also appears in the title of Note XXVII (R239/E156). As the metaphor at the end of the poem will imply, the Firebird may be understood as alcohol. Animal motif. Alcohol theme.

История разворачивается в царстве, где неизвестный крадет яблоки из королевского сада. Трем принцам нужно найти вора. Младший, Иван-царевич, замечает, что дивная Жар-птица крадет яблоки, но ему удается поймать лишь пару ее перьев. Король изумляется их красотой и поручает сыновьям захватить Жар-птицу, в чем, в конце концов, преуспеет лишь Иван-царевич. Однако на пути назад он решает отдохнуть, и, преисполненные завистью, братья решают убить его. С помощью друга-волка у Ивана-царевича удается вернуться и восстановить порядок в царстве. Мотив воровства и фигура волка (в фольклоре являющемуся положительным персонажем, согласно известному совесткому фольклористу Владимиру Проппу) не чужды и роману Соколова. text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
As Yakov gazes out of his window and watches the world and people beyond it, he pretends to be checking the temperature.
ru_trans: Выглядывая из окна и наблюдая за находящимися за его пределами миром и людьми, Яков притворяется, что он якобы проверяет температуру.

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Elena Kravchenko draws a parallel between Bruegel and William Carlos Williams's *[Pictures from Bruegel](https://www.fadedpage.com/books/20191144/html.php)* here: "On the macro-level, the body of the verse section forms a circular arrangement, based on the annual cycle, examined earlier in the chapter. While on the micro-level of individual poems the movement of eternal return is created through a 'shaggy dog tale' structure. This technique harks back to another ekphrastic evocation of Brueghel. William Carlos Williams wrote a cycle of poems, entitled Pictures from Brueghel (1962), wherein each poem represents an ekphrasis of a Brueghel painting. In his ekphrasis Williams reconstructs the outline of Brueghel’s paintings, as if following the viewer's eye in motion. Sokolov's homage to Brueghel's pictorial technique conceals reflections of/on Williams's representation of Brueghel, in which figures 'Disciplined by the artist | to go round | & round'. Adopting the manner of a 'shaggy dog tale', many of Iakov’s poems indeed go round and round" (*The Prose* 64).

text: Ilya uses Yakov's patronymic as a familiar form of address. However, another reading would be that now that the possibility of Ilya being Yakov's father has been established, Alfeev (Yakov) is referred to by his patronymic. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Yakov returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

text: Boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
ru_trans: Ботинки. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает более двадцати видов обуви, встречающихся в трех романах Соколова: “башмаки, ботфорты, боты, ботинки (полуботинки), чеботы, чизмы, чубуры, галоши (калоши), геты, ичиги, кеды, клоги, лапти, мокроступы, обуви (обувки), сапоги, сандалии, тапочки (полутапочки), шлепанцы, штиблеты, тапти, туфли, валенки. Список можно расширить, включив такие атрибуты, как носки, чулки, портянки, гамаши, коньки, костыли и протезы” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Что касается Между собакой и волком, он замечает, что фамилия Ильи сразу наталкивает на мысль о хрустальных туфельках Золушки. Джонсон подчеркивает, что “мотив обуви — дань Соколова, будь то осознанная или неосознанная, традициям русской литературы, представленным его предшественниками — И. Буниным и В. Катаевым” (179). В интервью с А. и Н. Воронелями, Соколов называет Бунина и Гоголя своими “современниками, сотрудниками по цеху, старшими мастерами” (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Мотив обуви.

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Cinema. The Lumière brothers, Auguste Marie Louis Nicolas Lumière (19 October 1862 – 10 April 1954) and Louis Jean Lumière (5 October 1864 – 6 June 1948), were French manufacturers of photography equipment and filmmakers. They are best known for the invention of the cinématographe, a three-in-one device that could record, develop, and project motion pictures. The original cinématographe had been patented by Léon Guillaume Bouly on 12 February 1892, and the device was further developed by the Lumières, who patented their own version on 13 February 1895. The Lumières went on to produce short films between 1895 and 1905, and they may have organized the very first presentation of projected film. Audiences, it turned out, preferred projected films, which could be viewed by many people at once, to “peepshow” devices like Thomas Edison’s kinetoscope, which only allowed one viewer at a time. Here, “Monsieur Lumière” may refer exclusively to Louis Lumière, who was more involved in the invention of the cinématographe than his brother.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text:
Elena Kravchenko writes: "If writing is a communication with the absent, text, like speech, is rooted in presence: in the presence of the other, the addressee that makes it meaningful. This aspect of the text is brought to the fore by Ilya, playfully
wishing 'whoever' a happy Sunday/Resurrection, which in Russian is denoted by the same word [...] Ilya's narrative is presented in the form of *skaz*, a particular technique of literary presentation of the spoken word. As it imitates an oral account, not only is *skaz* infused with living speech, it
also presupposes an addressee. Ilya's *skaz* is also a letter, read by the addressee posthumously, as it turns out: a remainder, a trace of the loss, endowed with meaning by absence. Absence is turned into a potential space, a playground, where the interchange between the self and the other, the inner and the outer, can be borne without the anguish of being annihilated or annihilating. *Between
Dog and Wolf* creates a space between writing and reading, held by the doubles of the voice that captivates us and the silence without which we would not be able to hear it" ("*Between Dog and Wolf*" 278).
ru_trans: Е. Кравченко объясняет: "Если письмо — общение с отсутствующим, то текст, подобно речи, основывается на присутствии: осмысление происходит в присутствии другого лица, адресата. Этот аспект текста на первый план выводит Илья, игриво желая "кому угодно" счастливого воскресенья/Воскресения, в русском языке обозначающимися одним словом. [...] Повествование Ильи представляется в форме сказа —  произведении русского фольклора. Подражая устной речи, сказ не только имитирует бытовой говор, но и предполагает наличие адресата. Сказ Ильи также является и письмом, попадающим к адресату, как это выясняется, посмертно: остаток, след утраты, смысл которому дает отсутствие. Отсутствие превращается в потенциальное пространство, игровую площадку, где чередование между собой и чужим, внутренним и внешным можно вынести без того, чтобы уничтожить или быть уничтоженным. "Между собакой и волком" формирует пространство между письмом и чтением, удерживаемое удвоением завораживающего нас голоса тишиной, без которой бы мы его не услышали" ("Between Dog and Wolf" 278).

text: Mentioned four times in the novel with different surnames (R153/E7, R199/E89, R242/E161, R278/E225). The name of Arabic origin Aladdin (Al al-Din) means “nobility of faith” and was popularized by the success of *One Thousand and One Nights*, before the 1992 homonymous Disney movie. Here it is used to suggest the Tatar origin of the character (directly indicated in Note XIV). His last name is mentioned alternatively as Batrutdinov and Rakhmatullin: the first derives from the Arabic name Batrutdin which means “full moon of the faith”; the second is a Tatar or Bashkir last name, derived from the name Rahmatullah, “mercy of God.” In previous editions: "Рахматуллин".

Здесь оно используется как намек на татарское происхождение героя (прямо раскрывается в Записке 15). Фамилия упоминается или как Батурдинов, или как Рахматуллин: первая происходит от арабского имени Батрудин, означающего "полнолуние верности"; вторая — татаро-башкирская фамилия, произошедшая от имени Рахматулла, "милость Божья". text: Oak forest. Mikhail Epstein notes that in Russian poetry “the oak tree is separated from the other trees, which makes it the king of the tree kingdom. It embodies the highest degree of hardness, courage, strength and majesty. It is this clarity of the original meaning that made the image of the oak tree especially popular in the early stages of poetry, and then weakened its significance when the imagery of poetry began to become more complex and overcome the unambiguity of folklore and allegorical musings. […] The oak tree in Russian poetry, as well as in world folklore, symbolizes the power of life that overcame death; that is why the decay of the oak tree acts as an ominous sign of the collapse of life, the invasion of demonic forces in its sanctuary” (47, 50). text: Elena Kravchenko reads this phrase as a "disturbing" metaliterary reference and as an address to the reader: "Sidor Fomich Pozhilykh is whoever *you* are, turned into a character for novelistic convenience. In a Borgesian revelation, the reader of Il'ia's outpourings finds himself fictionalized into the investigator, facing a happy 'voskresenie', a word which signifies both Sunday and resurrection in Russian. Il'ia's spirit is 'resurrected' through its consumption by the reader. This transubstantiation is performed through the evocation of the Holy Communion, in which text becomes wine, which becomes blood (and flesh)" (*The Prose* 84).
