text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Ilya names Yakov as his son. Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.

text: Ilya wishes the inspector a happy resurrection, suggesting once again a cyclical idea of life and death. In chapter 9 Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, was "‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, The Resurrection of the Elderly. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh 'a happy resurrection': this is his final message, his 'good news'. It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (good news) – in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical 'blagaia vest’' in 'blagoe izvestie'” (Napolitano, "Studyin" 286).

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Yakov returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Отчество Якова Алфеева намекает на то, что его отец — Илья. Однако данная интерпретация представляется спорной. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает: "Яков — сын Ильи: в такой же степени, как и всё в сумеречном мире меж собакой и волком. Тем не менее, и Яков, и Илья не имеют ни малейшего подозрения об этом, и когда их дальнейшие жизни в качестве точильщика и собаковода окончательно и бесповортно пересекаются, они в равной степени и не знают о своей скоротечной дружбе в больнице (…). [Яков] воссоздает образ хромого Эдипа. Он невольно убивает и отца, и (хоть и не буквально) "женится" на копии своей матери. Соколов переосмыслил и инсценировал греческую трагедию об Эдипе в верховьях Волги" (“Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212).  Действительно, Илья будет убит Яковым в качестве отомщения за то, что первый (в сумерках, пересекая замороженную реку) ошибочно принимает одну из собак последнего за волка и убивает ее. После того, как охотник крадет его костыли, Илья возвращается, чтобы убить собак. Для более подробного ознакомления с мифопоэтикой Соколова см. работу И. В. Ащеуловой "Творчество Саши Соколова в контексте литературного процесса 60–80-х".

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья здесь обращается к себе в третьем лице. Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
ru_trans: Ботинки. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает более двадцати видов обуви, встречающихся в трех романах Соколова: “башмаки, ботфорты, боты, ботинки (полуботинки), чеботы, чизмы, чубуры, галоши (калоши), геты, ичиги, кеды, клоги, лапти, мокроступы, обуви (обувки), сапоги, сандалии, тапочки (полутапочки), шлепанцы, штиблеты, тапти, туфли, валенки. Список можно расширить, включив такие атрибуты, как носки, чулки, портянки, гамаши, коньки, костыли и протезы” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Что касается Между собакой и волком, он замечает, что фамилия Ильи сразу наталкивает на мысль о хрустальных туфельках Золушки. Джонсон подчеркивает, что “мотив обуви — дань Соколова, будь то осознанная или неосознанная, традициям русской литературы, представленным его предшественниками — И. Буниным и В. Катаевым” (179). В интервью с А. и Н. Воронелями, Соколов называет Бунина и Гоголя своими “современниками, сотрудниками по цеху, старшими мастерами” (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Мотив обуви.

text: A reference to Ivan Turgenev's 1852 cycle of short stories *Notes of a Hunter* (also translated as *A Sportman's Notebook*, *The Hunting Sketches*, and *Sketches from a Hunter's Album*). This work was acclaimed for its portrayal of peasant life. The "Notes" (Записки) trope is common in Russian literature: *Notes of a Rifle Hunter* (Aksakov), Notes of a Shallow Grass (Dryansky), "Notes of a Madman" (Gogol), *Notes from the Underground* (Dostoevsky), *Notes from a Dead House* (Dostoevsky), "Notes of a Madman" (Tolstoy), "Notes of a Christian" (Tolstoy), *Notes of a Doctor* (Veresaev), *Notes of a Young Doctor* (Bulgakov), *Notes of a Psychotic* (Ven. Erofeev), and *Notes of a Nonhunter* (Vantalov). Gerald Smith suggests that the Drunken Huntsman may also be a literary descendent of Alexander Pushkin's hero in *The Gypsies* ("The Verse" 329).

text: Ostanin identifies this as an allusion to Mikhail Lermontov's 1837 poem "Borodino": "Что ж мы? на зимние квартиры?" (35). Read the poem and an English translation [here](https://ruverses.com/mikhail-lermontov/borodino/1830/). Responding to a question regarding similarities between his style and that of Vladimir Nabokov, Sokolov said, "I've surmized that a similarity in our styles might come from a common source: We share favorite writers. It may be enough to point to Gogol' and Lermontov. By connecting these two, a system of coordinates appears, from which one can determine style. Of course, only if both writers are favorites" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 353). For more on Sokolov and Nabokov, see D. Barton Johnson's "Saša Sokolov and Vladimir Nabokov." There, the critic writes, "After arriving in Vienna in October 1975, Sokolov read (in Russian) *Lolita* and *The Gift* and was surprised to note similarities between the avant-garde prose style of *Škola dlja durakov* and Nabokov's prose techniques […] Dismayed, Sokolov determined to develop a new, distinctive voice, one not under the shadow of the older writer. This search led to the exotic language of his 1980 *Meždu sobakoj i volkom*" (154). Evgeny Sokolov calls *Between Dog and Wolf* a "poema squared," riffing on Gogol's characterization of his novel *Dead Souls* as a poema (10).

into an old barrel? It will tear apart all its seams, it will warp 
the thing, and, what’s even worse, it will spill out
text: A reference to the parable of new wine into old wineskins found in [Luke 5:36–39](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%205%3A36-39&version=NIV;RUSV): "And he spake also a parable unto them; No man putteth a piece of a new garment upon an old; if otherwise, then both the new maketh a rent, and the piece that was taken out of the new agreeth not with the old. And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish." This line has entered the Slavic canon also thanks to the "[Sermon of Law and Grace](http://sites.utoronto.ca/elul/English/218/Ilarion.pdf)" attributed to Hilarion (XI century), where we read: "Ибо не вливают, по словам Господним, вина учения нового, благодатного в мехи ветхие, обветшавшие в иудействе: прорываются мехи, и вино вытекает." On another level, this line is suggestive of Sokolov's approach to art. That is, new forms (proetry, for example) are necessary to express new content, much as *Between Dog and Wolf* challenges readers with its innovative style and form. Of course, pairing Yakov (the Drunken Huntsman) with Hilarion is a debatable and possibly ironic choice. In an interview with Ivan Podshivalov, Sokolov said the following regarding Alexander Solzhenitsyn: "Solzhenitsyn tries: He writes; he makes an effort to keep pace with new literary current. He obviously takes pains to adopt new forms, assimilate avant-garde devices, but none of that suits him. Is it possible to pour new wine into old wineskins" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 356). On the subject of "proetry" and genre, Sokolov had the following to say: "Genres boundaries have eroded, and there is not need to reestablish them. The time has come for a new period of synthesis. As I explained genre interests me less than the kinds of works I write. I create *proetry* (*proezia*). This term is my discovery. Although, of course, I am far from being the first, and, more likely, I am the last in a long line of followers of the tradition that includes Turgenev and Bunin. Earlier, there were verses in prose, yet it remained prose. I think of myself as a proet" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 352). Elsewhere, however, Sokolov has expressed a view that underscores literary lineage: "For me language is a kind of symphony, and it works out that I'm writing variations on its themes. I don't think that in principle something new comes out of it. You can only dream of something new. Anyone who writes is limited by the nature of speech" (Litus, "Snezhnyi" 382). On the use of poetry in prose, see [Artem Skvortsov's article "Iavivshiesia v inom oblichii: o poezii v proze."](https://magazines.gorky.media/october/2018/9/yavivshiesya-v-inom-oblichii.html)

text: According to Boguslawski's annotations, *zimar'* refers to Andrei Voznesensky's poem "Song-travesty from the spectacle 'Antiworlds'" (1963) ("Annotations" 233). text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Dated/dialectical: bast shoe, rope shoe, galosh. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Set expression: to die suddenly. The phrase refers to the Cossack ataman Kondratii (Kondrashka) Bulavin who led an uprising in 1707–1708 in Russia. Most often this expression is used humorously to show the absurdity of a certain situation. Nowadays, the phrase is used figuratively, denoting confusion and surprise. Historian V. Solovyov suggested that the expression originated after Kondraty Bulavin's revolt of 1707. The Don Cossack ataman organized a popular uprising, which at a certain stage was very successful. Yuri Dolgorukov (1664-1707) and his army were sent by Peter I to subdue the Cossacks. Kondraty Bulavin defeated the detachment of Dolgorukov, taking him prisoner and delivering him to a shameful execution. The protégé of Peter I had his head cut off, and a bold letter was sent to the tsar: “Kondrashka Bulavin took Dolgorukov."
ru_trans: Устойчивое выражение: внезапно умереть. Фраза относится к казацкому атаману Кондратию (Кондрашке) Булавину, возглавлявшему восстание 1707–1708 годов в России. Чаще всего это выражение употребляется в юмористическом смысле, чтобы показать нелепость какой-либо ситуации. В современном языке фраза употребляется в переносном смысле, обозначая замешательство и удивление. Историк В. Соловьев предположил, что выражение возникло после восстания Кондратия Булавина 1707 года. Донской казачий атаман организовал народное восстание, которое на определенном этапе имело большой успех. Юрий Долгоруков (1664-1707) со своим войском был отправлен Петром I для усмирения казаков. Кондратий Булавин разбил отряд Долгорукова, взял его в плен и предал позорной казни. Протеже Петра I отрубили голову, а царю отправили смелое письмо: "Кондрашка Булавин Долгорукова хватил".

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Yakov returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). text: Ostanin (43) suggests interpretинг his last name as a variation of "Palamakherov" (from the verb palit', to burn), meaning someone who starts (or stops) fires. On that note, it would be worth recalling that final lines of the novel are, "So I dare you to burn, you dumb-as-a-bell, / My amazing, ingenious lines!" text: Gury's first appearance. Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). Animal motif.

text: Original Russian: челнок (*chelnok*). A dugout canoe. Also appears above in Note XXVIII. Boat motif.

Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in this chapter it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it will be Krylobyl in chapter 14 who Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise." In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

Это неудивительно, ведь его "говорящее имя" образовано словами "крыло" и "был". text: Originally (since the XI century) the khorunzhy was a military rank identifying the standard-bearer (khorugv' means heraldic flag) in military units of armies of many Slavic countries, later (since the XIV century) a commander of a military unit in medieval Poland and Lithuania. In the XVI-XVIII centuries it was also the name of an army official in the Zaporizhian Sich and other Cossack communities. There existed a general (troop), a regimental and a centurion khorunzhy, who were part of the Cossack senior officers and performed duties related to the organization of gatherings and inspections of troops, accounting of weapons, storage of flags, etc.. The khorunzhy was also the name of a junior officer rank in the Cossack troops of pre-revolutionary Russia (since the 18th century), corresponding to the rank of lieutenant and cornet in the regular Russian Imperial army. Emel'yan Pugachyov (leader of a major popular uprising under Catherine II) was a khorunzhy.

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). Animal motif.

The [region known as Valdai Hills](https://www.google.com/maps?output=search&q=Valdai+Hills&entry=mc&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjIuqK9yPj-AhUpLFkFHat1BusQ0pQJegQIDBAB). text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен (*paklen*) and неклен (*neklen*) are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Neklina, Paklina). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). text: According to Boguslawski, a "paraphrased quote from Vladimir Sokolov's untitled 1967 poem 'Na vlazhnye planki ogrady' (On the wet planks of the fence)" ("Annotations" 236). Read the poem (in Russian) [here](https://liricon.ru/na-vlazhnye-planki-ogrady.html). In the poem, two people have a conversation by a fence. It is the beginning of autumn, and it is raining. The first speaker asks whether the other person likes this weather, “When it drizzles, drizzles… / And the yellow eye on the water, / The streetlamp because of the branches squints”. The second responds that they like it, “That they (both) are, as in their youth, delirious, / That their coat smells like rain.” They like it, but they decide to leave, to go where no one knows. The last stanza of the poem describes how, for a long time at the fence, “where seconds drip into the tub," fragments of that conversation like leaves rustle and rustle.

text: In these lines and others, the connection between the mythic hoopoe and Ilya the knife-grinder become clearer: "The hoopoe shares Ilya’s profession of grinding, moves about on one leg, and lives in the same space as his human counterpart among the other invalids of Gorodnishche. In a transmutation of the Tereus myth, the cutting of Philomela’s tongue echoes Ilya-hoopoe’s association with 'scythes, or sickles, or axes,' as well as the loss of his leg on a railroad track at some point in the novel (at least a couple variants of the story are given). In this case, of course, it is the man who suffers the dismemberment, but the cycle of violence from the original myth finds resonance in *Dog*’s plot where no bad deed goes unreciprocated" (Vergara, "Flap" 366). text: Sokolov explains: "In the years we are talking about, many houses were not, pardon the expression, gasified, and in many kitchens people cooked on kerosene stoves, AKA kerosinki, which made those kitchens and the adjoining premises smell of kerosene fumes. This smell is nostalgic to me: it brings back memories of that unpretentious, poor, but in its own way cozy life of communal houses and dachas of the forties and fifties. At that time and later in the city courtyards in the evenings there was an interesting life: neighbors played soccer, dominoes, cards, sang guitar songs, drank hot drinks, discussed news and gossiped. An individual walking through the courtyard became an object of attention, a familiar person was greeted, an unfamiliar one was silently looked at to discuss who he was, how he was dressed and where he was going. In general, the courtyard community was interested in every passerby, noticed and met everyone in one way or another. They would meet them if the weather was good. In this case, the weather is bad - damp, slushy, probably windy, and the barracks, i.e. the population, the people of the barracks, will not meet the jubilant centipede, because the courtyard is empty, everyone is at home, no one wants to catch a cold, get polyps in the nose or inflammation of the glands. I did not use this term, I used a colloquial variant, usually this problem is interpreted simply: he had, let's say, tonsils, i.e. inflammation of the tonsils. Or a case like this: the medical report says 'he died of a myocardial infarction', but the neighbors say: 'of heart'. I dare to explain why fragments of bottle glass do not shine either at the pier or in garbage heaps: [a certain critic admired Chekhov's ability to describe natural phenomena and landscapes](https://proza.ru/2013/10/12/967?ysclid=lkq42bv7s5481764198) very laconically and gave an example: in a certain story Chekhov, to make it clear that the night is moonlit, offers one detail: a fragment of bottle glass shines near the pier" (personal communication, July 29, 2023).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

Пастернака Доктор Живаго, где корень фамилии главного героя — “жив” (жить) (Ostanin 10). Прочитать оригинал можно здесь. Он также отмечает, что А. Пушкин намеревался включить рассказ “Записки старика” в его цикл рассказов Повести Белкина. Прочитать оригинал можно здесь, а английский перевод — здесь. Как замечает М. Наполитано, “Пожилых, адресат Ильи, перевоплощается в картину Воскресения, чье название играет с двусмысленностью его фамилии – Воскресение Пожилых. Илья действительно завершает свое письмо пожеланием Пожилых “счастливого воскресения”; таково его последнее послание, его “благая весть”. Это в буквальном смысле его Евангелие, от греческого εὐαγγέλιον (добрая весть); в оригинале Илья искажает каноническое “благая весть” в “благое известие” (Napolitano, “Studyin” 286).

text: The mythical Firebird from Slavic folklore. Read the original [here](https://xn----7sbb5adknde1cb0dyd.xn--p1ai/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/) and an English translation [here](http://www.artrusse.ca/fairytales/firebird.htm). The story is set in a kingdom where an unknown thief is stealing apples from the king’s garden. The three princes must find out who is the thief: the younger, Ivan, observes that it is a marvelous Firebird stealing the apples, but he is only able to catch one of the bird’s feathers. The king is amazed by its beauty and orders his sons to capture the Firebird, an adventure that will be successful in the end only for Ivan. However, on his way back, he takes a rest and his brothers, out of envy, decide to kill him. Thanks to the help of a wolf friend, Ivan manages to recover and reestablish order in the kingdom. The motif of theft and the figure of the wolf (in the folk tale, a positive hero according to Vladimir Propp, famed Soviet folklorist) are relevant to Sokolov’s novel, too. The Firebird also appears in the title of Note XXVII (R239/E156). As the metaphor at the end of the poem will imply, the Firebird may be understood as alcohol. Animal motif. Alcohol theme.

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Boris Ostanin also notes that in the Koran the hoopoe turns up late to King Solomon's congress of birds but manages to escape the death sentence after he explains that he was spying in Queen Sheba's kingdom; Solomon then sends the hoopoe with a message to Sheba (39). In this way, additional links between the myth and Ilya are activated: Ilya's letter to Pozhilykh sent after his own murder at the hands of Yakov, mail, an escape from death (Vergara, "Flap" 367). Animal-human motif.

text: Pine. As Mikhail Epstein notes, "Pines and spruce trees represent part of a gloomy, harsh landscape; wilderness, darkness, and silence reign around them. [...] Pines and spruces mean not only the peace of sleep, but also the peace of death. If an oak tree that has grown over a grave is a symbol of eternal life overcoming death, then the pine tree is perceived as a tombstone erected by nature itself over a person and confirming the hopelessness of death […]. The pine tree stands out for its slenderness and height, which allows it to 'converse' with the wind. One of the most persistent poetic motifs is pine trees swayed by the wind like bells, causing a ringing sound throughout the forest [...]. The slenderness of pine trunks gives reason to compare them with columns and strings" (75–76, 80). Plant motif.

Если дуб, выросший над могилой,— сим­вол вечной жизни, преодолевающей смерть, то сосна воспринимается как надгробье, воздвигнутое самой при­родой над человеком и подтверждающее безысходность кончины […]. text: Boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.

text: Quail. According to Beryl Rowland, the quail has been equated with salacious women (*Birds* 140). "The erotic significance," Rowland continues, "dates from ancient times, when the bird was a symbol of generation and rebirth. Latona, the goddess who gave birth to Artemis and Apollo at Delos, regarded the bird as her own: the Phoenician Hercules, whose death and resurrection were commemorated annually, was revived when the quail, a bird 'noted for its pugnacity and lechery,' was held to his nose. The same significance may explain the story of the migrating quails in [Exodus xvi.13](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%2016%3A13-16&version=NIV,NRT) and [Numbers xi.33-34](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers+11%3A33-34&version=NIV;NRT). [...] In the ninth century Rabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mainz, in commenting on the passage, declared, "by quail is meant the pleasures of the body" (141). Alternatively, Peter Tate writes that quails have been associated with Biblical plagues, the taste of their flesh and eggs, unwholesomeness, and medicinal qualities (107–108). The birds in this scene greedily collect the Sower's seeds. Animal motif.

text: Lilies. According to Ernst and Johanna Lehner, the lily has long been "the sacred flower of motherhood," and in "ancient Semitic legend, the lily sprang from the tears of Eve, when expelled from the Garden of Eden she found she was approaching motherhood. In later Christian lore it was said that the lily had been yellow until the day the Virgin Mary stooped to pick it. IN Christian symbolism the lily represented purity, chastity and innocence, and is the symbol of resurrection and Easter" (32). Plant motif.

text:
Elena Kravchenko writes: "If writing is a communication with the absent, text, like speech, is rooted in presence: in the presence of the other, the addressee that makes it meaningful. This aspect of the text is brought to the fore by Ilya, playfully
wishing 'whoever' a happy Sunday/Resurrection, which in Russian is denoted by the same word [...] Ilya's narrative is presented in the form of *skaz*, a particular technique of literary presentation of the spoken word. As it imitates an oral account, not only is *skaz* infused with living speech, it
also presupposes an addressee. Ilya's *skaz* is also a letter, read by the addressee posthumously, as it turns out: a remainder, a trace of the loss, endowed with meaning by absence. Absence is turned into a potential space, a playground, where the interchange between the self and the other, the inner and the outer, can be borne without the anguish of being annihilated or annihilating. *Between
Dog and Wolf* creates a space between writing and reading, held by the doubles of the voice that captivates us and the silence without which we would not be able to hear it" ("*Between Dog and Wolf*" 278).

text: The mythical Firebird from Slavic folklore. Read the original [here](https://xn----7sbb5adknde1cb0dyd.xn--p1ai/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/) and an English translation [here](http://www.artrusse.ca/fairytales/firebird.htm). The story is set in a kingdom where an unknown thief is stealing apples from the king’s garden. The three princes must find out who is the thief: the younger, Ivan, observes that it is a marvelous Firebird stealing the apples, but he is only able to catch one of the bird’s feathers. The king is amazed by its beauty and orders his sons to capture the Firebird, an adventure that will be successful in the end only for Ivan. However, on his way back, he takes a rest and his brothers, out of envy, decide to kill him. Thanks to the help of a wolf friend, Ivan manages to recover and reestablish order in the kingdom. The motif of theft and the figure of the wolf (in the folk tale, a positive hero according to Vladimir Propp, famed Soviet folklorist) are relevant to Sokolov’s novel, too. The Firebird also appears in the title of Note XXVII (R239/E156). As the metaphor at the end of the poem will imply, the Firebird may be understood as alcohol. Animal motif. Alcohol theme.

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Animal-human motif.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. text: This event is later recounted in chapter 14 by Ilya, but there *he* is the furrier under the stairs (R255/E187). D. Barton Johnson summarizes: "Orina's story has strange echoes in Il'ya's later life. After parting from Orina, Il'ya sets himself up as a fur-dresser/cobbler [...] Living in a room beneath the stairs, he befriends an old woman rag-picker and her mentally retarded ward whom he seduces when she brings him an animal hide. Their assignations take place in his room and under a beached boat, but the relationship ends when the pregnant girl takes up with the local sailors [...] The fox-fur slippers made for Orina by her cobbler-seducer foreshadow the unknown article made by cobbler Il'ya for the slow-witted girl who is Orina's successor" ("The Galoshes Manifesto" 153–164). Olga Matich reads Sokolov's novel as an extended response to Boris Pilnyak's short story "Mother Earth" (1927), as it shares confusion between a wolf and a fox, a character name Arina, and a setting on the Upper Volga, among other similarities ("Sasha Sokolov" 312–313). Read the original [here](http://az.lib.ru/p/pilxnjak_b_a/text_1924_mat_syra_zemlya.shtml).

Расставшись с Ориной, Илья становится меховщиком/сапожником […] Живя в комнате под лестницей, он сближается со старушкой-тряпичницой и ее умственно отсталой подопечной, которую он соблазняет, когда та приносит ему звериную шкуру. text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).
