text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. [от Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.

text: Foot wraps traditionally worn before the widespread use of socks in armies. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Yakov returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он - юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: Chorea — a movement disorder belonging to the  dyskinesias group of neurological disorders. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek "χορεία" and was used to described the movements of those inflicted by the disease. Sokolov's first novel, *A School for Fools*, is dedicated to Vitia Pliaskin, which refers to Sydenham's chorea (also known as "St. Vitus's dance, пляска святого Вита in Russian). Watch a video [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTCnbga3sqg). Referred to several times in the novel (R171, 191, 205, 214, 215/E37, 74, 97, 113, 115).

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. [от Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Ilya returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."
ru_trans: Отчество Якова Алфеева намекает на то, что его отец — Илья. Однако данная интерпретация представляется спорной. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает: "Яков — сын Ильи: в такой же степени, как и всё в сумеречном мире меж собакой и волком. Тем не менее, и Яков, и Илья не имеют ни малейшего подозрения об этом, и когда их дальнейшие жизни в качестве точильщика и собаковода окончательно и бесповортно пересекаются, они в равной степени и не знают о своей скоротечной дружбе в больнице (…). [Яков] воссоздает образ хромого Эдипа. Он невольно убивает и отца, и (хоть и не буквально) "женится" на копии своей матери. Соколов переосмыслил и инсценировал греческую трагедию об Эдипе в верховьях Волги" (“Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212).  Действительно, Илья будет убит Яковым в качестве отомщения за то, что первый (в сумерках, пересекая замороженную реку) ошибочно принимает одну из собак последнего за волка и убивает ее. После того, как охотник крадет его костыли, Илья возвращается, чтобы убить собак. Для более подробного ознакомления с мифопоэтикой Соколова см. работу И. В. Ащеуловой "Творчество Саши Соколова в контексте литературного процесса 60–80-х".

text: At this point, Yakov's voice begins to sound very much like that of Ilya. Again, the implication is that Yakov is the author of all parts of the novel and that he has been imitating Ilya. Elena Kravchenko writes, "Attributed to Iakov, who self-consciously adopts the tone and language reminiscent of Il'ia's *skaz*, the monologue discloses a possible source of the latter's voice: Makar Devushkin, a character of Fedor Dostoevskii's novel-in-letters, *Bednye liudi* (*Poor Folks*). Here, again, Sokolov resorts to a complex intertextual chain by bringing into play Dostoevskii's text, which is an acknowledged 'parody' (imitation) of Gogol''s style" (*The Prose* 70). Yakov has previous been associated with the magpie, which is significant as this bird has traditionally been "considered a symbol for poets thanks to the Roman satirist Martial, who wrote, 'I, a loquacious magpie, greet you with intelligible speech, my lord, and were you not to see me you would refuse to believe that I was a bird" (Martial, quoted in Rowland, *Birds* 105). As José Vergara explains, "This trait and classical link clearly align with Yakov, who is not only the thieving huntsman who takes Ilya’s crutches in response to the latter’s assault on his dog, but also the author of the poems […] In these poems, as elsewhere, he demonstrates a particular talent for 'imitat[ing] words in a distinct voice like men,' that is, he adopts various identities, voices, registers, and so on, as if chattering away like a magpie who responds to the people around him. Many of his poems consist of parodies and stylizations of nineteenth-century Russian poetry. Yakov incorporates bits and pieces of previous authors’ works in these texts, along with their general styles, rhythms, and so on. The prose chapters that concern him, but which are not narrated by him, also include ekphrastic descriptions of paintings ('Pictures from an Exhibition') and an account of his ancestor, Nikodim Yermolaich Palamakhterov, that reads as if lifted straight from Gogol. Much like Ilya’s hoopoe with its positive and negative connotations and Orina’s lapwings, who are closely tied to a sexuality that is both weaponized and treasured, the Yakov-magpie pairing is therefore multivalent, and it contributes to Sokolov’s art of blended identities. On the one hand, Yakov’s personality, his originality, becomes lost in this mirror-like text. On the other, he takes joy in his chameleon-esque nature […] Although Yakov constructs his poetic 'nest' deep in the Volga backwoods out of borrowed materials, the resulting product, like that of the magpie, is nevertheless highly original. Yakov’s literary theft involves the recontextualization of his stolen materials, which transforms them significantly" ("Flap" 370–371). In a letter addressed to his publisher Carl Proffer in August 1976, Sokolov admitted being dissatisfied with the first parts of the novel he sketched and explained the reason for this unsuccessful result in this way: "I began to sing in a voice that was not mine" (University of California Santa Barbara. Sasha Sokolov collection, Mss 117 Box 1: 5–6). As Martina Napolitano suggests, "Sokolov’s second novel […] was born out of a reflection on the structuring role of narrating voices" ("Studyin" 281). Animal-human motif.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Foma Pogibel' is one of the two oarsmen who carry people (dead or alive) across the river (a variation of the Charon Greek myth). The other oarsman is Eryoma (diminutive of Eremei, Jeremiah). However, in Note XXXI the oarsman is called Pavel, just like the character who sends his uncle Pyotr to get yeast in Gorodnishche. As underlined by one of the epigraphs in Sokolov’s first novel, *A School for Fools*, the biblical name of Pavel is somehow interchangeable: “Saul, who is called Paul” (see [Acts 13:9–10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). As for Foma, he carries a biblical name, too (Thomas), whose Aramaic origin suggests the idea of the “twin.” This apostle is famous as “Doubting Thomas” due to his denial of the resurrection of Jesus, according to the Gospel of John (see [John 20:24–31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). In the Orthodox tradition, the Sunday following Easter is called “Thomas Sunday”: the day when Christ appeared to his disciples; it took seeing Jesus’ body for Thomas to name him “My Lord and my God.” Foma Pogibel''s "portrait" appears in Note XXIII (R231–232/E142–143).

text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Yakov mentions in Note 2 that the "lonesome babe" chides him for abandoning his boots (R165/E29). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Yakov suggests that he sees Bruegel's painting outside his window. A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of *The Pictures*, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement […] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's *[The Census at Bethlehem](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg)* (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

text: Elena Kravchenko suggests that these lines can be read as "a loose 'paraphrase' of chapter 4, stanza 35 from Alexander Pushkin's novel-in-verse *Evgenii Onegin* (*The Prose* 57). Read the original [here](http://www.poetry-classic.ru/4-35.html) and an English translation [here](http://lib.ru/LITRA/PUSHKIN/ENGLISH/onegin_j.txt). Olga Matich writes: "If the realists Turgenev, Aksakov, and abovementioned painters represented reality, Khlebnikov transforms it by means of futurist discourse. Sokolov, in turn, may be said to transform it into metaliterature, which is self-reflexive in relation to both language and writing more generally. [...] To summarize, “Eclogue” represents a parodic cluster whose intertexts are both obvious and implied that require interpretation and knowledge of Russian literary history, including the inscription of archaic forms (“*svoiasi*”), all of which are prominent in the novel. Significantly, the poem references the ubiquitous wolf – here as a visual metaphor of a wolf fang resembling a young moon – as well as a dog.We may also claim that “Eclogue” is Sokolov’s parodic pastiche of his own novel" ("*Between Dog and Wolf*" 256).
ru_trans: Е. Кравченко предполагает, что данные строки могут быть прочтены как вольный "пересказ" части 4, станзы 35 романа в стихах "Евгений Онегин", написанного Александром Пушкиным ("The Prose" 57). С оригиналом можно ознакомиться [здесь](http://www.poetry-classic.ru/4-35.html). О. Матич пишет: "Если реалисты Тургенев, Аксаков и вышеупомянутые художники изображали действительность, то Хлебников трансформирует ее посредством футуристского дискурса. Соколов, в свою очередь, можно сказать, превращает ее в мета-литературу, саморефлесивную по отношению и к языку, и к письму в целом. [...] Подводя итог, можно сказать, что что 'Эклога' представляет собой пародийный кластер, интертекстуальность которого как ясна, так и подразумевает необходимость понимания и знания истории русской литературы, в том числе и вписывания архаических форм ('свояси'), занимающих важное место в романе. Примечательно, что стихотворение упоминает вездесущих волка —здесь в виде визуальной метафоры вольчего клыка, напоминающего молодую луну, — и собаку. Можно также утверждать, что 'Эклога' — пародийный патиш Соколова на его собственный роман" ("Between Dog and Wolf" 256).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).
ru_trans: Необычная несклоняемая фамилия, буквально означающая “старый, старик”. Останин подчеркивает возможную связь с романом Б. Пастернака Доктор Живаго, где корень фамилии главного героя — “жив” (жить) (Ostanin 10). Прочитать оригинал можно здесь. Он также отмечает, что А. Пушкин намеревался включить рассказ “Записки старика” в его цикл рассказов Повести Белкина. Прочитать оригинал можно здесь, а английский перевод — здесь. Как замечает М. Наполитано, “Пожилых, адресат Ильи, перевоплощается в картину Воскресения, чье название играет с двусмысленностью его фамилии – Воскресение Пожилых. Илья действительно завершает свое письмо пожеланием Пожилых “счастливого воскресения”; таково его последнее послание, его “благая весть”. Это в буквальном смысле его Евангелие, от греческого εὐαγγέλιον (добрая весть); в оригинале Илья искажает каноническое “благая весть” в “благое известие” (Napolitano “Studyin” 286). Пожилых переносится из одного уровня повествования (письмо Ильи следователю) в другой (повествование о жизни и воображении Якова от третьего лица). Более того, он включен в выдуманную сцену из жизни французской королевской семьи.

text: The Pavel Bure (Paul Buhre) watch company was established in 1874 (although the family had started this activity back in 1815). In 1899 Pavel Bure was given the title of "court supplier to the Emperor" (between 1887 and 1917 the Russian court bought more than 10,000 watches from his factory). Bure watches are mentioned in many literary works, for example by Anton Chekhov, or Il'f and Petrov in their *The Golden Calf*. After the 1917 Revolution the Bure factory stopped its activity in Russia, but continued to work in Switzerland.

text: Another ekphrastic description of *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, the first appearance of which occurs in chapter 2. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of *The Pictures*, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.
ru_trans:
Это стихотворение — очередное экфрастическое описание написанной в 1565 году картины Питера Брейгеля Старшего "Охотники на снегу". Сцена из картины повторяется на протяжении "Между собакой и волком" (например, R202–203/E93–95), будто бы оживая на страницах романа. 
Е. Кравченко объясняет: "Помимо метафоры посещения художественной выставки, приема экфрасиса и 'галерейной' структуры 'Картинок', Соколов заимствует основополагающую телеологию творчества Мусоргского. Наравне с Бородиным, Балакиревым, Кюи и Римским-Корсаковым, Мусоргский относился к 'Могучей кучке'. Созданная под патронажем художественного критика В. Стасова, группа стала эпицентром развития нового национального стиля русской музыки, в основе которого лежали крестьянские традиции и фольклор. Могучая кучка была тесно связана и черпала вдохновение у художественного движения Передвижников […]. Яков намерен передать ту же идею. Он поселяется на Волге, чтобы запечатлить и отобразить жизнь тамошних людей. Помимо поэтического дара, Яков также наделен художественным талантом, и это его работы формируют словесную галерею прозаических глав. 'Экспонаты' галереи или графически выделены курсивом, то есть, относятся к названию картины, или определяются отсылкой к 'прототипу' образа" ("The Prose" 61). Она продолжает: "Можно предположить, что изображение Яковом человеческого страдания, что является одной из главных тем романа и что было определено как одно из центральных моральных посылов картин Брейгеля, строится не напрямую на Брейгеле, а на экфрасисе У. Одена в его ['Музее изящных искусств'](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt). Останавливаясь на ['Переписи в Вифлееме'](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg (1566) и ['Избиении младенцев'](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg) (пр. 1564) Брейгеля, экфрасис достигает кульминации в описании ['Падения Икара'](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg) (пр. 1558)" ("The Prose" 63). О присутствии и роли образов и подтекстов Брейгеля можно прочитать в статье М. Карамитти "[Мультифильмы Брейгеля"](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) (Caramitti, “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia”). Помимо этих очевидных экфрастических связей между романом Соколова и картиной Брейгеля, стоит отметить и другие моменты. Например, серия из которой взяты "Охотники на снегу", "Времена года" (1565) состоит из шести картин, пять из которых сохранились до наших дней. "Если деление года на шесть картин поначалу кажется странным, — пишут С. Пено и Э. Оберталер, — то это утверждает себя как общепринятый в Нидерландах того времени способ погружения в годовой цикл, так как различались весна ранняя и нет, раннее лето и середина лита. Присущая году цикличность упраздняет дискуссию о 'правильном' порядке картин — какая картина представляет собой начало серии, а какая — конец" (214). То же самое может быть сказано и о структуре "Между собакой и волком", где поэтические главы прослеживают развитие сезонных изменений, в то время как все существует в промежуточном состоянии (времена года, личности персонажей и т. д.). Стоит также отметить, что как и в тексте Соколова, где не соблюдается строгое следование географической реальности, пейзажи, изображенные на картинах "Времен года", не являются точными: "Эти так называемые 'смешанные пейзажи' сочетают в себе воспоминания об Альпах с типично фламандскими мотивами" (229). Есть что сказать и отом, как Соколов, подобно Брейгелю, развивает "неисчерпаемое богатство деталей", которое неизбежно приводит к "пределам визуального восприятия и языковой репрезентации" (215). Одна деталь картины, явно не описанная Соколовым в романе, кажется релевантной: "Толстые сосульки облепили мельничное стекло у правого края и остановили его, слово бы само время замерло" (228). И действительно, в мире "Между собакой и волком" время, а значит и персонажи, чувствуют себя застрявшими.

text: A diminutive form of Krylobyl's name. Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in this chapter who Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise." In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен (*paklen*) and неклен (*neklen*) are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Neklina, Paklina). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

Могучая кучка была тесно связана и черпала вдохновение у художественного движения Передвижников […]. Яков намерен передать ту же идею. Он поселяется на Волге, чтобы запечатлить и отобразить жизнь тамошних людей. Помимо поэтического дара, Яков также наделен художественным талантом, и это его работы формируют словесную галерею прозаических глав. "Экспонаты" галереи или графически выделены курсивом, то есть, относятся к названию картины, или определяются отсылкой к "прототипу" образа" (Kravchenko, "The Prose" 61). Она продолжает: "Можно предположить, что изображение Яковом человеческого страдания, что является одной из главных тем романа и что было определено как одно из центральных моральных посылов картин Брейгеля, строится не напрямую на Брейгеле, а на экфрасисе У. Одена в его "[Музее изящных искусств](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)". Останавливаясь на "[Переписи в Вифлееме](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg)" Брейгеля (1566) и "[Избиении младенцев](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)" (пр. 1564), экфрасис достигает кульминации в описании "[Падения Икара](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)" (пр. 1558)" (Kravchenko, "The Prose" 63). О присутствии и роли образов и подтекстов Брейгеля можно прочитать в [статье М. Карамитти "Мультифильмы Брейгеля"](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) (Caramitti “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia”).

In a letter dated February 24, 1981, D. Barton Johnson asked Sokolov, "Could you say something about the construction of the *Kartinki* sections? Are they all conceived as pictorial daydreams of the future artist as he (Jakov?) gazes out the schoolroom window?" In his response, dated March 3, 1981, Sokolov explains how in the "alcoholic imagination of the unsuccessful artist and poet-graphomanic" Yakov the landscape and human and non-human figures of Bruegel's *Hunters in the Snow* is superimposed on what he sees around him: "Yakov imagines (in the sense of dreams, or, rather, day-dreams) all his paintings, which he *could* paint, and it's as if Bruegel's *Hunters in the Snow* is one of his own paintings. But in the Note that's called "To the Unknown Painter" (I think that's what it is; I don't have the book with me — I lent it) Yakov the poet criticizes Bruegel, whom he *doesn't know*, for his inaccurate representation of Gorodnishche and the hunters' clothings (and so on)." Sokolov explains that for Yakov all of life is "day-dreaming," and the paintings in his imagination blend together as if in a "kaleidoscope" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).
ru_trans: В письме от 24 февраля 1981 года Д. Бартон Джонсон спросил Соколова: "Не могли бы Вы прокомментировать структуру 'Картинок'? Они все задуманы как живописные грезы будущего художника, пока он (Яков?) глядит в окно из школьного окна?" В своем ответе от 3 марта 1981 года Соколов объясняет, как в "алкогольном воображении неудавшегося художника и поэта-графомана" Якова пейзаж и человеческие и нечеловеческие фигуры брейгелевских "Охотников на снегу" накладываются на то, что он наблюдает вокруг себя: "Яков воображает (в смысле dreams, or, rather, day-dreams [мечт/снов или, скорее, дневных грез]) все свои картины, которые он *мог бы* написать, и 'Охотники на снегу' Брейгеля — как бы одна из его собственных картин. Но в Записке, кот[орая] называется "К Незнакомому Живописцу" (кажется так; у меня здесь нет книги — дал почитать) Яков-поэт критикует *незнакомого* ему Брейгеля за неточность изображения Городнища и одежды охотников (и т. д.), — Брейгеля, а м. б. и себя самого как соавтора (воображаемого) картины, Якова-художника. Остальные *якобы* — картины *Якова* — целиком вымышлены им в процессе жизни и day-dreaming, да вся жизнь для него, художника и пьяницы по натуре, это —day-dreaming. И картины его воображения (а часто и воспоминания) переливаются, переходят одна в другую, это — калейдоскоп" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).

Leona Toker was an early observer of the day-dream qualities of Yakov's character and of the novel as a whole. As she wrote in a letter to D. Barton Johnson dated March 26, 1985, "Part of it is, overtly, day-dreaming; and day-dreaming involves a co-presence of different and often contradictory variants of the same story, variants that emerge in accordance with the pscyhological [sic] urges at different times of one's life and that somehow do not cancel the earlier versions that they contradict. This, might be one of the ways to account for the structure of the novel. At the same time the novel is free from the sugary (*pritornyi*) wish-fulfilling quality (as of Aksyonov's slicks) of day-dreams. Rather it has the rough, knobly, prickly, smarting surface which makes it seem so true and which I greatly enjoyed" (Box 13, Folder 1, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).
ru_trans: Л. Токер была одним из первых наблюдателей мечтательных качеств характера Якова и романа в целом. Как она написала в письме к Д. Б. Джонсону от 26 марта 1985 года: "Часть его — откровенные мечтания наяву; а те предполагают соприсутствие различных и часто противоречивых вариантов одной и той же истории, вариантов, которые возникают в соответствии с психологическими [исправлено] побуждениями в разные периоды жизни человека и которые каким-то образом не отменяют более ранние версии, которым они противоречат. Может быть, это один из способов объяснить структуру романа. В то же время роман свободен от приторного исполнения желаний (как в аксёновской чересчур отшлифованной прозе) мечтаний.
