text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен (*paklen*) and неклен (*neklen*) are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Neklina, Paklina). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text:
A short pastoral poem often featuring a dialogue between shepherds. Alexander Pushkin mentions the genre in his novel-in-verse *Eugene Onegin* in [chapter 3 stanza 2](http://www.poetry-classic.ru/3-2.html). Elena Kravchenko describes the poem's technique as follows: "The technique of the ‘Eclogue’ draws on the parodic tradition of cento, a verse
composition made up of famous lines selected from the works of the past. A collage of voices, disposed in a new form or order, cento functions as parodic defamiliarization, refracting the intentions of originals. In the ‘Eclogue’ it is achieved through the juxtaposition of ‘polar’ opposites such as Khlebnikov and Turgenev, whose discourses produce the most improbable dialogue, and through the superimposition of the sign onto the alleged referent. This principle is captured in the poem’s title, ‘Eclogue’. The genre of the eclogue suggests a poem written in a classical style on a pastoral subject. Trans-contextualizing a classical verse into his novel, Sokolov creates a comic clash between the poem’s claims at bucolic bliss and the novel’s setting that starkly communicates a picture of the post-war devastation of provincial Russia. As has been noted, in its evocation of the pastoral, Sokolov’s poem is not a parody of the classical genre per se, but of the endeavour to compare artistic discourse about reality with reality itself. Moreover, it is not a simple parody of the truth-searching, but a parody of a parody: Iakov’s undertaking to compare the discourse of cultural ‘authorities’ with the real world is conceptualized through the evocation of his ‘precursors’, Don Quixote and Emma Bovary" (*The Prose* 58).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the Zaitil'shchina, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: The name Emeli'an (Emil) is derived from the Latin aemulus which means rival, literally "emulator." In this context, it's a fitting name given the relationship between Ilya and his brother, as well as the fluid nature of the divisions between characters' identities. Aemilianus was also briefly Roman emperor in 253. Ostanin notes that Emel'yan was also the name of Pugachev, a Cossack ataman who led a popular insurrection during the reign of Catherine the Great (52). His figure turned literary thanks to Pushkin and his historical novel *The Captain's Daughter* (1836). In Pushkin’s novel, Pugachev is described through the eyes of the nobleman Grinev who dislikes this illiterate “drunkard” wandering outlaw, yet does not refuse him his hareskin coat as a token of his gratitude. During the first Russo-Turkish war (1768–1774) Pugachev served in the Russian army as *khorunzhy*, a military rank mentioned in chapter 3.
ru_trans: Имя Емельян (Эмиль) образовано от латинского *aemilianus*, что означает "соперник", буквально "эмулятор" ("подражатель"). В данном контексте, это отлично подходящее имя, учитывая отношения между Ильей и его братом, а также размытые границы между личностями персонажей. Эмилиан также недолго был римским императором в 253 году. Останин замечает, что Емельяном также звали казацкого атамана, предводителя крупного восстания во время правления Екатерины Великой (Ostanin 52). Его образ стал литературным благодаря Пушкину и его исторической повести "Капитанская дочка" (1836). В романе Пушкина Пугачев описывается глазами дворянина Гринева, который недолюбливает этого безграмотного "пьяницу", бродягу-разбойника, но не отказывает ему в заячьей шубе в знак благодарности. Во время первой русско-турецкой войны (1768–1774) Пугачев служил в русской армии хорунжим — это воинское звание упоминается в главе 3.

Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: Yakov suggests that he sees Bruegel's painting outside his window. A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой *Между собакой и волком* и автор того, что он называет *Заитильщиной* — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на [Приволжье](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе  (Johnson “Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition*” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (Johnson “Twilight Cosmos” 644).

Olga Matich writes of the sewing themes: "Yet the verb “weave” and noun “weaving” appear only rarely in the novel
and only with its meaning defamiliarized or rewoven, for example in the wellknown colloquial idiom in which weaving words is a metaphor for speaking nonsense ('Ой, плетете вы сами не знаете что,' 142), perhaps intended as
a parody of word-weaving. Another estranged usage is that of '*pleten'*' (wattle fence) metamorphosed into a thrice removed distant relative ('троюродный плетень,' 112); or '*spletni*' (108), meaning gossip, which comes from the verb 'spletat’' (weave in the sense of intertwine). The altercation between Ilya
and the wolf on the ice inscribes reweaving (*perepletat*) rendered as 'Мудрено индивиду в таких переплетах баланс удерживать' (139) [...] '*Pereplet*' means book binding, with its plural in this passage metaphorized as a situation in which Ilya finds it difficult to keep his balance on the ice. The phrase, I would suggest, may also be a nod to *Between Dog and Wolf*’s readers who sometimes find it very difficult to interpret that which they encounter between its, so to speak, woven, rewoven, or interwoven 'bindings'" (*Between Dog and Wolf* 255–256).

text: A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement […] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his 'Musée des Beaux Arts'. Running through the images of Brueghel's *[The Census at Bethlehem](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg)* (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of [*Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg) (ca. 1558)" (The Prose 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also Mario Caramitti’s article “[Mul’tfilmy Breigelia](https://www.openstarts.units.it/server/api/core/bitstreams/91ab62b1-20af-4e0c-ba32-e45c7baeaf2d/content).” Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow derives*, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Sasha Sokolov explains that this expression should be intended "in a metaphoric and ironic way." He adds: "Holy fools and beggars belong to their own group, their own mafia. They live well thanks to charity. By common agreement, each one works in a strictly defined area: one controls the train station, one controls the cemetery, and one sits near the shopping center. The church porch is considered the most profitable place: believers are generous. The most influential and respected holy fools, veterans of the profession, operate on the porch. The porch is the highest level of the career ladder. Having occupied this position, the holy fool becomes an indispensable element of parish life until the end of the century; he becomes almost a staff member of the church, although he is not on any official list and does not receive a salary" (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Саша Соколов объясняет, что это выражение нужно понимать "в переносном и в ироническом смысле." Он добавляет к этому: "У юродивых и просто нищих - своя компания, своя мафия. Они неплохо живут благодаря подаяниям. По общему уговору, каждый работает на своем строго определенном участке: тот контролирует вокзал, тот кладбище, а этот - сидит возле торгового центра. Самым доходным местом считает церковная паперть: верующие щедры. На паперти подвизаются самые влиятельные и уважаемые юродивые, ветераны профессии. Паперть - высшая ступень карьерной лестницы. Заняв эту позицию, юродивый до скончания века становится непременным элементом приходской жизни, он делается как бы штатным сотрудником церкви, хотя ни в каком официальном списке не числится и зарплату не получают" (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

Devoted believers in Christianity who give up their possessions and behave in ways contrary to social standards in order to commit fully to their faith and to demonstrate the hypocrisies of society. Holy fools are common in Russian literature, both in religious texts and secular works.

text: Ilya cannot forget Orina and this makes the woman suffer. Ilya uses the same verb he used to describe himself getting thinner and thinner ("sokhnu", I dry up), but while in regard to himself this process is linked with his living a hard life, here the woman accuses him to make his flesh "dry up." text: Transformations, in general, are common in the novel. More specifically, here, the reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. The event is documented in [Matthew 17:1–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2017%3A1-8&version=NIV), [Mark 9:2–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark%209%3A2-8&version=NIV), and [Luke 9:28–36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%209%3A28-36&version=NIV). Celebrated on August 6. Here the transfiguration is also a metaphor suggesting Nikolai's death, which was previously described in chapter 1 by Ilya (R153/E8). The main character of Mikhail Bulgakov's *Heart of a Dog* (a novel which widely circulated in samizdat in the 60s) is Doctor Preobrazhensky, whose experiment of turning a homeless dog into a man leads to tragic consequences (and to his "transfigurating" back into a dog).
ru_trans: Преображения, в целом, нередко встречаются в романе. Там, на вершине, он начинает сиять, а рядом с ним появляются пророк Илия (одна из личностей Ильи в романе) и Моисей, в то время как к нему взывает Божий голос. Это событие описано в [Матфея 17:1-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+17%3A1-8&version=RUSV), [Марка 9:2-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+9%3A2-8&version=RUSV), [Луки 9:28-36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+9%3A28-36&version=RUSV). text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans:
Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также статью Т. Цвиян "Николай Угодник — странник на русской земле" 59).

text: French: *bilboquet*. The game cup and ball in which the player attempts to land a cup in a ball or a piece with a hole upon a stick. The game itself has a long history, and it is difficult to attest its first invention. It was extremely popular across the 16–18th centuries in Europe. A famous version of the game is the Japanese Kendama, based on the bilboquet first introduced during the Edo period (early 17th century).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: The narrator here suggests that it's the circumstances determine a thing's appearance, character, and so on, rather than the other way around. In other words, different contexts will generate different phenomena, much as the characters and settings in the novel shift depending on how their parts and configurations have been arranged around them. In short, a suggestion that art is self-defining.

text: Maple. As Ostanin notes, Sokolov was born in Canada, whose official emblem is the maple leaf (113). Epshtein explains that "Unlike the oak, the maple and the poplar trees do not have such a definite, formed figurative nucleus in Russian poetry. The fact is that even in folklore traditions associated with ancient pagan rituals, these trees did not play such a significant role. Poetic visions of them are mainly formed in the twentieth century [...]. If the oak is a representative of stout vitality, it is a kind of king and a man among the trees, then the maple is a frivolous guy, a little crazy, with an exuberant pile of uncombed hair [...]. The image of the maple is most developed in the poetry of Sergei Yesenin, where it acts as a sort of lyrical hero of the 'wood novel.' The image of the maple tree as a country boy, a walker, a suitor is most clearly depicted [...]. Another stable figurative motif associated with the maple is the toothedness of its leaves, which remotely resemble the shape of a heart, making the maple as if it were the patron saint of love [...]." Here Epstein mentions in particular works by Fet, Blok, Zabolotsky, Akhmatova. “The Maple is often associated with the concept of chastity, purity. In Fet's poetry the maple is said to be ‘virgin,' in Blok's it is 'fresh,' in Pasternak's there is 'not even a speck in the new maples…’” (50–53). Plant motif.
ru_trans: Как отмечает Останин, Соколов родился в Канаде, официальный символ которой —кленовый лист (113). Эпштейн поясняет, что "в отличие от дуба, клен и другие тополи не имеют такого определенного, сформировавшегося образного ядра в русской поэзии. Дело в том, что даже в фольклорных традициях, неотрывно связанных с древними языческими ритуалами, эти деревья не играли значительной роли. Поэтические представления о них формируются в основном в XX веке [...]. Если дуб, будучи представителем крепкой жизненной силы, является своего рода королем среди деревьев, клен, в таком случает, выступает как легкомысленный и слегка сумасшедший парень с буйной копной нечесаных волос [...]. Образ клена наиболее развит в поэзии Сергея Есенина, где он становится своеобразным лирическим героем 'лесного романа'. Другой устоявшийся образ клена — зубчатость его листьев, отдаленно напоминающих форму его сердца, отдаленно напоминающих форму сердца; это превращает клен в некого святого покровителя любви [...]". Здесь Эпштейн упоминает, в частности, произведения Фета, Блока, Заболоцкого, Ахматовой. "Клен зачастую ассоциируется с идеей целомудрия, чистоту. В поэзии Блога клен 'девственен', у Блока — 'свеж', а у Пастернака он описывается так: 'в новых кленах нет ни пятнышка...'" (50-53). Мотив растений.

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

text: According to D. Barton Johnson, this was the first poem written by Sokolov for the novel. It was written in July 1976 on a train between Zürich and Locarno ("Background Notes" 338). Indeed, in a letter dated March 3, 1981, wrote the following to his friend and critic: "I had a premonition of the book, a forefeeling—the general contours, an outline, if you will. The poems appeared on their own. I wrote the first poem on a train, on the way from Zürich to Locarno, in July 76. That was Note IX, which parodies Pushkin's style. It seems to have been successful, although in Sov[iet] criticism there's a widespread opinion that it's impossible to parody Pushkin, because it's like parodying the Russian language itself" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections). Railroad theme.
ru_trans: По словам Д. Бартона Джонсона, это было первое стихотворение, написанное Соколовым для романа. Оно было написано в июле 1976 года в поезде между Цюрихом и Локарно (Johnson, "Background Notes" 338). Действительно, в письме от 3 марта 1981 года Соколов написал следующее своему другу и критику: "У меня было предчувствие книги, предощущение — и общий контур, абрис, если угодно. Стихи появились сами. Первое стихотворение написал в поезде, по дороге из Цюриха в Локарно, в июле 76 года. Это была Записка IX, пародирующая пушкинский стиль. Кажется, удалась, хотя в сов[етской] критике распространено мнение, что Пушкина пародировать невозможно, ибо это все равно, что пародировать сам русский язык" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections). text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh, The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (good news); in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical blagaia vest’ in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

Olga Matich writes: "If the realists Turgenev, Aksakov, and abovementioned painters represented reality, Khlebnikov transforms it by means of futurist discourse. Sokolov, in turn, may be said to transform it into metaliterature, which is self-reflexive in relation to both language and writing more generally. [...] To summarize, “Eclogue” represents a parodic cluster whose intertexts are both obvious and implied that require interpretation and knowledge of Russian literary history, including the inscription of archaic forms (“*svoiasi*”), all of which are prominent in the novel. Significantly, the poem references the ubiquitous wolf – here as a visual metaphor of a wolf fang resembling a young moon – as well as a dog.We may also claim that “Eclogue” is Sokolov’s parodic pastiche of his own novel" ("*Between Dog and Wolf*" 256).

text:
A short pastoral poem often featuring a dialogue between shepherds. Alexander Pushkin mentions the genre in his novel-in-verse *Eugene Onegin* in [chapter 3 stanza 2](http://www.poetry-classic.ru/3-2.html). Elena Kravchenko describes the poem's technique as follows: "The technique of the ‘Eclogue’ draws on the parodic tradition of cento, a verse
composition made up of famous lines selected from the works of the past. A collage of voices, disposed in a new form or order, cento functions as parodic defamiliarization, refracting the intentions of originals. In the ‘Eclogue’ it is achieved through the juxtaposition of ‘polar’ opposites such as Khlebnikov and Turgenev, whose discourses produce the most improbable dialogue, and through the superimposition of the sign onto the alleged referent. This principle is captured in the poem’s title, ‘Eclogue’. The genre of the eclogue suggests a poem written in a classical style on a pastoral subject. Trans-contextualizing a classical verse into his novel, Sokolov creates a comic clash between the poem’s claims at bucolic bliss and the novel’s setting that starkly communicates a picture of the post-war devastation of provincial Russia. As has been noted, in its evocation of the pastoral, Sokolov’s poem is not a parody of the classical genre per se, but of the endeavour to compare artistic discourse about reality with reality itself. Moreover, it is not a simple parody of the truth-searching, but a parody of a parody: Iakov’s undertaking to compare the discourse of cultural ‘authorities’ with the real world is conceptualized through the evocation of his ‘precursors’, Don Quixote and Emma Bovary" (*The Prose* 58).

text: Another ekphrastic description of *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, the first appearance of which occurs in chapter 2. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of *The Pictures*, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement […] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's *[The Census at Bethlehem](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg)* (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

text: The reference here is to the Red Guards (Hong Weibing), a student-let movement who supported Mao during the first phase of the Cultural Revolution (1960s). In the USSR they were known as “khunveybiny” in the media. As Ostanin recalls (69), they used to cut political opponents' “dogs’ heads" (69). Here, the allusion could also remind a Russian reader of the typical symbol of the oprichniki (a dog’s head, along with a broom), Ivan the Terrible's police force. Animal motif.
ru_trans: Отсылка к Красногвардейцам — студенческому движению в поддержку Мао во время первой стадии Культурной революции (1960-е). В СССР они стали известны в СМИ как "хунвэйбины". Как замечает Останин, они рубили "собачьи головы" партийным оппозиционерам (Ostanin 69). Этот образ также может напомнить русскому читателю о эмблеме опричнины (собачья голова с метлой) — вооруженных сил силы Ивана Грозного. Мотив животных.

text: Hanna Kolb suggests that "yesterday's sensations" are "chimerical" and that this "mixture of newspaper stories from throughout the world are obviously pseudo-news mocking the sensation-seeking of historical thought, and mixing in anachronistic play the old, the new and the timeless" ("The Dissolution" 199). Asked to comment on this specific passage, Sokolov answered: "All of these episodes are related to events that happened in the nineteenth century. I used newspaper headlines, titles from old publications I once found in some library. I have some knowledge of some of the events but not of all of them. I know nothing about the meeting of the emperors in [Hoštejn](https://www.google.com/maps/place/789+01+Ho%C5%A1tejn,+Czechia/@49.8765466,16.774945,15z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x47120e9ccb59fcb1:0x400af0f66151810!8m2!3d49.8743822!4d16.7747719!16s%2Fm%2F076wd3v?entry=ttu) [Boguslawski translates this small Czech village as Holstein, which is instead Germany]. The criminal actions of bashi-bazouks towards Bulgarians took place more than once in different years; these repressions became one of the reasons of the Russian-Turkish war of 1877–78. In general, Russia fought Turkey many times. Tsai Hsun was a prince and head of the Ministry of Naval Affairs. I couldn't find anything else about him. The evacuation of Russian troops from Manchuria took place in 1902. The Casablanca incident took place in the nineteenth century and has nothing to do with the movie, but what the incident was is unclear" (personal communication, July 7, 2023). He also suggests readers consider the articles available at [these](https://warspot.ru/4039-na-shipke-vsyo-spokoyno) [two](https://dzen.ru/a/Y8Zx7PJJYTFnaHGj) websites in order to learn more about, respectively, the (ironic) expression "All is calm on Shipka" pronounced by Russian general Fyodor Radetsky in 1877, at a time when he was stoically sharing the deprivations of his men during the Siege of Shipka Pass, and the figure of Tsai Hsun.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги, также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если *Школа для дураков* была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, *Между собакой и волком* можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в *Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву* и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (Johnson 217).

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He's a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it was Krylobyl who advanced the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it will be Krylobyl in chapter 14 who Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise." In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

Note XVII

To the Unknown Painter
text: This poem is yet another iteration of the ekphrastic description of *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf*, as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

The woodpecker has traditionally played roles "as the god-sent bird in the ancient sacred grove; as the bird who [...] cared for Romulus and Remus, and as the oracular bird of Mars, god of war" (Rowland, *Birds* 180). text: In a letter dated February 24, 1981, D. Barton Johnson asked Sokolov, "Could you say something about the construction of the *Kartinki* sections? Are they all conceived as pictorial daydreams of the future artist as he (Jakov?) gazes out the schoolroom window?" In his response, dated March 3, 1981, Sokolov explains how in the "alcoholic imagination of the unsuccessful artist and poet-graphomanic" Yakov the landscape and human and non-human figures of Bruegel's *Hunters in the Snow* is superimposed on what he sees around him: "Yakov imagines (in the sense of dreams, or, rather, day-dreams) all his paintings, which he *could* paint, and it's as if Bruegel's *Hunters in the Snow* is one of his own paintings. But in the Note that's called "To the Unknown Painter" (I think that's what it is; I don't have the book with me — I lent it) Yakov the poet criticizes Bruegel, whom he *doesn't know*, for his inaccurate representation of Gorodnishche and the hunters' clothings (and so on)." Sokolov explains that for Yakov all of life is "day-dreaming," and the paintings in his imagination blend together as if in a "kaleidoscope" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).

text: Leona Toker was an early observer of the day-dream qualities of Yakov's character and of the novel as a whole. As she wrote in a letter to D. Barton Johnson dated March 26, 1985, "Part of it is, overtly, day-dreaming; and day-dreaming involves a co-presence of different and often contradictory variants of the same story, variants that emerge in accordance with the pscyhological [sic] urges at different times of one's life and that somehow do not cancel the earlier versions that they contradict. This, might be one of the ways to account for the structure of the novel. At the same time the novel is free from the sugary (*pritornyi*) wish-fulfilling quality (as of Aksyonov's slicks) of day-dreams. Rather it has the rough, knobly, prickly, smarting surface which makes it seem so true and which I greatly enjoyed" (Box 13, Folder 1, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections).
