text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Death. The reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. The event is documented in [Matthew 17:1–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2017%3A1-8&version=NIV), [Mark 9:2–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark%209%3A2-8&version=NIV), and [Luke 9:28–36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%209%3A28-36&version=NIV). Celebrated on August 6. The main character of Mikhail Bulgakov's *Heart of a Dog* (a novel which widely circulated in samizdat in the 60s) is Doctor Preobrazhensky, whose experiment of turning a homeless dog into a man leads to tragic consequences (and to his "transfigurating" back into a dog). Locally, this concept and its relationship to death also figures prominently in Note XVIII (R204–205/E95–96).

Это событие описано в [Матфея 17:1-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+17%3A1-8&version=RUSV), [Марка 9:2-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+9%3A2-8&version=RUSV), [Луки 9:28-36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+9%3A28-36&version=RUSV). text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги, также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если *Школа для дураков* была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, *Между собакой и волком* можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в *Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву* и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (Johnson 217).

text: Maple. As Ostanin notes, Sokolov was born in Canada, whose official emblem is the maple leaf (113). Epshtein explains that "Unlike the oak, the maple and the poplar trees do not have such a definite, formed figurative nucleus in Russian poetry. The fact is that even in folklore traditions associated with ancient pagan rituals, these trees did not play such a significant role. Poetic visions of them are mainly formed in the twentieth century [...]. If the oak is a representative of stout vitality, it is a kind of king and a man among the trees, then the maple is a frivolous guy, a little crazy, with an exuberant pile of uncombed hair [...]. The image of the maple is most developed in the poetry of Sergei Yesenin, where it acts as a sort of lyrical hero of the 'wood novel.' The image of the maple tree as a country boy, a walker, a suitor is most clearly depicted [...]. Another stable figurative motif associated with the maple is the toothedness of its leaves, which remotely resemble the shape of a heart, making the maple as if it were the patron saint of love [...]." Here Epstein mentions in particular works by Fet, Blok, Zabolotsky, Akhmatova. “The Maple is often associated with the concept of chastity, purity. In Fet's poetry the maple is said to be ‘virgin,' in Blok's it is 'fresh,' in Pasternak's there is 'not even a speck in the new maples…’” (50–53). Plant motif.
ru_trans: Как отмечает Останин, Соколов родился в Канаде, официальный символ которой —кленовый лист (113). Эпштейн поясняет, что "в отличие от дуба, клен и другие тополи не имеют такого определенного, сформировавшегося образного ядра в русской поэзии. Дело в том, что даже в фольклорных традициях, неотрывно связанных с древними языческими ритуалами, эти деревья не играли значительной роли. Поэтические представления о них формируются в основном в XX веке [...]. Если дуб, будучи представителем крепкой жизненной силы, является своего рода королем среди деревьев, клен, в таком случает, выступает как легкомысленный и слегка сумасшедший парень с буйной копной нечесаных волос [...]. Образ клена наиболее развит в поэзии Сергея Есенина, где он становится своеобразным лирическим героем 'лесного романа'. Другой устоявшийся образ клена — зубчатость его листьев, отдаленно напоминающих форму его сердца, отдаленно напоминающих форму сердца; это превращает клен в некого святого покровителя любви [...]". Здесь Эпштейн упоминает, в частности, произведения Фета, Блока, Заболоцкого, Ахматовой. "Клен зачастую ассоциируется с идеей целомудрия, чистоту. В поэзии Блога клен 'девственен', у Блока — 'свеж', а у Пастернака он описывается так: 'в новых кленах нет ни пятнышка...'" (50-53). Мотив растений.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Egor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. от [Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: Hanna Kolb suggests that "yesterday's sensations" are "chimerical" and that this "mixture of newspaper stories from throughout the world are obviously pseudo-news mocking the sensation-seeking of historical thought, and mixing in anachronistic play the old, the new and the timeless" ("The Dissolution" 199). Asked to comment on this specific passage, Sokolov answered: "All of these episodes are related to events that happened in the nineteenth century. I used newspaper headlines, titles from old publications I once found in some library. I have some knowledge of some of the events but not of all of them. I know nothing about the meeting of the emperors in [Hoštejn](https://www.google.com/maps/place/789+01+Ho%C5%A1tejn,+Czechia/@49.8765466,16.774945,15z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x47120e9ccb59fcb1:0x400af0f66151810!8m2!3d49.8743822!4d16.7747719!16s%2Fm%2F076wd3v?entry=ttu) [Boguslawski translates this small Czech village as Holstein, which is instead Germany]. The criminal actions of bashi-bazouks towards Bulgarians took place more than once in different years; these repressions became one of the reasons of the Russian-Turkish war of 1877–78. In general, Russia fought Turkey many times. Tsai Hsun was a prince and head of the Ministry of Naval Affairs. I couldn't find anything else about him. The evacuation of Russian troops from Manchuria took place in 1902. The Casablanca incident took place in the nineteenth century and has nothing to do with the movie, but what the incident was is unclear" (personal communication, July 7, 2023). He also suggests readers consider the articles available at [these](https://warspot.ru/4039-na-shipke-vsyo-spokoyno) [two](https://dzen.ru/a/Y8Zx7PJJYTFnaHGj) websites in order to learn more about, respectively, the (ironic) expression "All is calm on Shipka" pronounced by Russian general Fyodor Radetsky in 1877, at a time when he was stoically sharing the deprivations of his men during the Siege of Shipka Pass, and the figure of Tsai Hsun.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах ("Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Yakov suggests that he sees Bruegel's painting outside his window. A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в *Между собакой и волком*. Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (Johnson “Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти» (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, та дама (та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (Smith 333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка *Мать сыра-земля* (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (Matich “Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (Caramitti “Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (Caramitti “Amore e morte” 118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского «ignis» (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Паклиа* и *паклина* — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины *паклен* и *неклен* относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Как автор “Записок”, так и Илья по всей видимости или наслышаны о человеке по фамилии Паклин или знают его лично. Илья утверждает, что фамилия Арины была Неклина —  вероятно, унаследованная от одного из ее партнеров. И вот, спустя годы, как предполагает Илья, она живет с другим, чью фамилию ему подсказывает ему второе название дерева» (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023 г.).

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он — юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: Foma Pogibel' is one of the two oarsmen who carry people (dead or alive) across the river (a variation of the Charon Greek myth). The other oarsman is Eryoma (diminutive of Eremei, Jeremiah). However, in Note XXXI the oarsman is called Pavel, just like the character who sends his uncle Pyotr to get yeast in Gorodnishche. As underlined by one of the epigraphs in Sokolov’s first novel, *A School for Fools*, the biblical name of Pavel is somehow interchangeable: “Saul, who is called Paul” (see [Acts 13:9–10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). As for Foma, he carries a biblical name, too (Thomas), whose Aramaic origin suggests the idea of the “twin.” This apostle is famous as “Doubting Thomas” due to his denial of the resurrection of Jesus, according to the Gospel of John (see [John 20:24–31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). In the Orthodox tradition, the Sunday following Easter is called “Thomas Sunday”: the day when Christ appeared to his disciples; it took seeing Jesus’ body for Thomas to name him “My Lord and my God.”
ru_trans: Фома Погибель — один из двух перевозчиков, переносящих людей (мертвых или живых) через реку (аналог Харона, греческой реки мертвых). Еще один перевозчик — Ерема (уменьшительное от "Еремей"). Однако в Записке 31 имя перевозчика — Павел: такое же, как и у персонажа, пославшего своего дядю Петра за дрожжами в Городнище. Как подразумевается в одном из эпиграфов в первом романе Соколова, "Школа для дураков", бибилейское имя Павел заменяемо: "Савл, он же Павел" (см. [Деяния 13:9-10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). Фома тоже имеет библиейское имя (Томас), арамейское происхождение которого подсказывает идею "близнеца". Данный апостол известен как "Фома неверующий" из-за своего отрцания воскресения Иисуса, согласно Ивангелию от Иоанна (см. [От Иоанна 20:24-31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). В православной традиции воскресенье, следующее за Пасхой, называется "Фоминым воскресеньем": это день, когда воскресший Христос предстал перед своими учениками; Фоме потребовалось увидеть тело Иисуса, чтобы называть его "своим Господом и своим Богом". "Портрет" Фомы Погибеля появляется в Записке 23 (R231–232/E142–143).

text: Maple. As Ostanin notes, Sokolov was born in Canada, whose official emblem is the maple leaf (113). Epshtein explains that "Unlike the oak, the maple and the poplar trees do not have such a definite, formed figurative nucleus in Russian poetry. The fact is that even in folklore traditions associated with ancient pagan rituals, these trees did not play such a significant role. Poetic visions of them are mainly formed in the twentieth century [...]. If the oak is a representative of stout vitality, it is a kind of king and a man among the trees, then the maple is a frivolous guy, a little crazy, with an exuberant pile of uncombed hair [...]. The image of the maple is most developed in the poetry of Sergei Yesenin, where it acts as a sort of lyrical hero of the 'wood novel.' The image of the maple tree as a country boy, a walker, a suitor is most clearly depicted [...]. Another stable figurative motif associated with the maple is the toothedness of its leaves, which remotely resemble the shape of a heart, making the maple as if it were the patron saint of love [...]." Here Epstein mentions in particular works by Fet, Blok, Zabolotsky, Akhmatova. “The Maple is often associated with the concept of chastity, purity. In Fet's poetry the maple is said to be ‘virgin,' in Blok's it is 'fresh,' in Pasternak's there is 'not even a speck in the new maples…’” (50–53). Plant motif.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Egor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. от [Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: Alexander Sergeevich Pushkin (1799–1837), the father of modern Russian letters and a crucial source of subtexts in *Between Dog and Wolf*. In fact, the phrase "пора меж волка и собаки" (the time between wolf and dog") appears in Pushkin's celebrated novel-in-verse *Eugene Onegin* (ch. 4, stanza 47).

Transformations, in general, are common in the novel. More specifically, here, the reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. The event is documented in [Matthew 17:1–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2017%3A1-8&version=NIV), [Mark 9:2–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark%209%3A2-8&version=NIV), and [Luke 9:28–36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%209%3A28-36&version=NIV). Celebrated on August 6. Here the transfiguration is also a metaphor suggesting Nikolai's death, which was previously described in chapter 1 by Ilya (R153/E8). The main character of Mikhail Bulgakov's *Heart of a Dog* (a novel which widely circulated in samizdat in the 60s) is Doctor Preobrazhensky, whose experiment of turning a homeless dog into a man leads to tragic consequences (and to his "transfigurating" back into a dog).

text: An allusion to the story of how Alexander Pushkin, the father of Russian letters, encountered a hare on the road while on his way to support the Decembrist Revolt and took it as a bad omen. "Кучерявый" (curly), a trait Pushkin is well known for, further strengthens this allusion. At the end of the poem, the curly-headed quality will move from the hare to the lyric persona (line 100).

text: Nikolai's name shortens to Nikola. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Сокращенная форма имени "Николай". Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. The one-legged Ilya will be associated with the trapper who lives under the stairs and works with animal furs. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by  the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

Это неудивительно, ведь его "говорящее имя" образовано словами "крыло" и "был". text: The Yegor/Fyodor/Pyotr trio again. As seen in chapter 1 (R154/E10) and elsewhere, Pyotr's name (not necessarily identity) constantly alternates with Yegor and Fyodor. Again, a random assignment of names to characters. In this case, the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

text: The pre-revolutionary term for the Mari peoples. The Mari live along the Volga and Kama Rivers and in the Mari El, Bashkortostan, and Tatarstan Republics. Martina Napolitano writes, "In 1968 Sokolov eventually chose to register as a non-attending student (*zaochnoe obuchenie*) due to his frustration with city life. He moved to the village of Morki in the Mari Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic with Taisiia Suvorova, a fellow student and his first wife until 1974. He then concluded his studies in 1971, having already started to collaborate with the prestigious “Literaturnaia gazeta” mainly submitting book and art reviews. His last article published on the pages of this weekly magazine, titled *Poznat' prirodu tetivy* (Knowing the nature of the bowstring), was dedicated to Mari poets. In this text, Sokolov expressed his appreciation for the first translations that appeared in Russian, but also included general reflections concerning poetry and art" (*Sasha Sokolov*). In a review with Kira Sapgir, Sokolov stated the following: "“I believed that the work of a journalist would lead me faster to real prose. And since you can write more freely not in the central newspaper, but in a peripheral one, I switched to the correspondence department and left for the Mari Republic. I worked in a district newspaper, in a village, a hundred kilometers from Yoshkar-Ola. I was 22 years old. My appearance there — "a man from the capital" — was somewhat stunning. As a result, I wasn't bothered, and I could write whatever I wanted, I could even afford to experiment. I wrote mainly essays about people: I took the surname, first name, and patronymic of a person, and invented his whole life. These were, in fact, stories, and the hero could be a gamekeeper, forester, innkeeper, anyone. These were short story-essays written in rhythmic prose: if you like, close to the style of Andrei Bely, although at that time I hadn't read anything about him or his work itself. The first time I read Bely was here, abroad, and I was surprised: it looks similar" ("V 'Russkoi mysli'" 11).
ru_trans:
Дореволюционное название марийцев. Марийцы живут вдоль рек Волги и Камы, в Респубиках Башкорстан, Татарстан и Марий Эл. М. Наполитано пишет: “В 1968 году Соколов, разочарованный в городской жизни, в конце концов решил перейти на заочное обучение. Он переехал в деревню Морки в Марийской АССР вместе с Таисией Суворовой, однокурсницей и своей первой женой, с которой он был до 1974 года. В 1971 году он завершил свое обучение, уже начав сотрудничать с престижной 'Литературной газетой', в основном занимаясь написанием рецензий на книги и искусство. Его последний очерк, опубликованный на страницах этого еженедельного журнала, под названием 'Познать природу тетивы' была посвящена марийским поэтам. В этом произведении Соколов выразил свою признательность за первые переводы, появившиеся на русском языке, также приводя общие размышления о поэзии и искусстве” ("Sasha Sokolov"). В беседе с К. Сапгир Соколов делится: “Я считал, что работа в журнале быстрее подведёт меня к настоящей прозе. А поскольку свободно можно писать не в центральной газете, а в периферийной, я перешёл на заочное отделение и уехал в Марийскую республику. Работал я в районной газете, в селе, в ста километрах от Йошкар-Олы. Мне было двадцать два года. Моё появление там — 'человека из столицы' — было несколько ошарашивающим. В результате меня не правили, и я мог писать всё, что хотел, мог себе позволить даже экспериментировать. Писал, в основном, очерки о людях: брал фамилию, имя и отчество человека, а всю его жизнь выдумывал. Это были, в сущности, рассказы, а герой мог быть егерем, лесником, трактирщиком, кем угодно. Они были написаны ритмической прозой, если хотите, близкие к стилю Андрея Белого, хотя тогда я не читал ничего ни его, ни о нём. Впервые я прочитал Белого здесь, за границей, и удивился: похоже" ("V 'Russkoi mysli'" 11).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. text: Ostanin (43) suggests to interpret his last name as a variation of "Palamakherov" (from the verb palit', to burn), meaning someone who starts (or stops) fires. On that note, it would be worth recalling that final lines of the novel are "So I dare you to burn, you dumb-as-a-bell, / My amazing, ingenious lines!" ("Попробуй пожги только, дурья башка, / Мои гениальные строчки") (R280/E230). text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Dated: February. бок (side) + греть (to warm). As Boguslawski translates it, "side-warmer," meaning a shift in weather that will warm your sides. A reference to St. Sidor Bokogrei, whose day is celebrated on May 14/27. He was given this name, because it was said that bitterly cold northern winds would stop blowing on this date. Likewise, swifts and swallows would fly to Sidor with the approach of warm weather. However, people caution against taking the appearance of the first bird as a sure sign of the cold's departure, similar to the following clause. text: Foma Pogibel' is one of the two oarsmen who carry people (dead or alive) across the river (a variation of the Charon Greek myth). The other oarsman is Eryoma (diminutive of Eremei, Jeremiah). However, in Note XXXI the oarsman is called Pavel, just like the character who sends his uncle Pyotr to get yeast in Gorodnishche. As underlined by one of the epigraphs in Sokolov’s first novel, *A School for Fools*, the biblical name of Pavel is somehow interchangeable: “Saul, who is called Paul” (see [Acts 13:9–10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). As for Foma, he carries a biblical name, too (Thomas), whose Aramaic origin suggests the idea of the “twin.” This apostle is famous as “Doubting Thomas” due to his denial of the resurrection of Jesus, according to the Gospel of John (see [John 20:24–31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). In the Orthodox tradition, the Sunday following Easter is called “Thomas Sunday”: the day when Christ appeared to his disciples; it took seeing Jesus’ body for Thomas to name him “My Lord and my God.”
ru_trans: Фома Погибель — один из двух перевозчиков, переносящих людей (мертвых или живых) через реку (аналог Харона, греческой реки мертвых). Еще один перевозчик — Ерема (уменьшительное от "Еремей"). Однако в Записке 31 имя перевозчика — Павел: такое же, как и у персонажа, пославшего своего дядю Петра за дрожжами в Городнище. Как подразумевается в одном из эпиграфов в первом романе Соколова, "Школа для дураков", бибилейское имя Павел заменяемо: "Савл, он же Павел" (см. [Деяния 13:9-10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). Фома тоже имеет библиейское имя (Томас), арамейское происхождение которого подсказывает идею "близнеца". Данный апостол известен как "Фома неверующий" из-за своего отрцания воскресения Иисуса, согласно Ивангелию от Иоанна (см. [От Иоанна 20:24-31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). В православной традиции воскресенье, следующее за Пасхой, называется "Фоминым воскресеньем": это день, когда воскресший Христос предстал перед своими учениками; Фоме потребовалось увидеть тело Иисуса, чтобы называть его "своим Господом и своим Богом". "Портрет" Фомы Погибеля появляется в Записке 23 (R231–232/E142–143).

text: Mari: no, there is not. Martina Napolitano writes, "In 1968 Sokolov eventually chose to register as a non-attending student (*zaochnoe obuchenie*) due to his frustration with city life. He moved to the village of Morki in the Mari Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic with Taisiia Suvorova, a fellow student and his first wife until 1974. He then concluded his studies in 1971, having already started to collaborate with the prestigious “Literaturnaia gazeta” mainly submitting book and art reviews. His last article published on the pages of this weekly magazine, titled *Poznat' prirodu tetivy* (Knowing the nature of the bowstring), was dedicated to Mari poets. In this text, Sokolov expressed his appreciation for the first translations that appeared in Russian, but also included general reflections concerning poetry and art" (*Sasha Sokolov*). In a review with Kira Sapgir, Sokolov stated the following: “I believed that the work of a journalist would lead me faster to real prose. And since you can write more freely not in the central newspaper, but in a peripheral one, I switched to the correspondence department and left for the Mari Republic. I worked in a district newspaper, in a village, a hundred kilometers from Yoshkar-Ola. I was 22 years old. My appearance there — 'a man from the capital' — was somewhat stunning. As a result, I wasn't bothered, and I could write whatever I wanted, I could even afford to experiment. I wrote mainly essays about people: I took the surname, first name, and patronymic of a person, and invented his whole life. These were, in fact, stories, and the hero could be a gamekeeper, forester, innkeeper, anyone. These were short story-essays written in rhythmic prose: if you like, close to the style of Andrei Bely, although at that time I hadn't read anything about him or his work itself. The first time I read Bely was here, abroad, and I was surprised: it looks similar" ("V Russkoi mysli" 11).

Он переехал в деревню Морки в Марийской АССР вместе с Таисией Суворовой, однокурсницей и своей первой женой, с которой он был до 1974 года. В 1971 году он завершил свое обучение, уже начав сотрудничать с престижной 'Литературной газетой', в основном занимаясь написанием рецензий на книги и искусство. text: Pyotr. Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. от [Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). text: Mari: is not. The Mari live along the Volga and Kama Rivers and in the Mari El, Bashkortostan, and Tatarstan Republics. Martina Napolitano writes, "In 1968 Sokolov eventually chose to register as a non-attending student (*zaochnoe obuchenie*) due to his frustration with city life. He moved to the village of Morki in the Mari Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic with Taisiia Suvorova, a fellow student and his first wife until 1974. He then concluded his studies in 1971, having already started to collaborate with the prestigious “Literaturnaia gazeta” mainly submitting book and art reviews. His last article published on the pages of this weekly magazine, titled *Poznat' prirodu tetivy* (Knowing the nature of the bowstring), was dedicated to Mari poets. In this text, Sokolov expressed his appreciation for the first translations that appeared in Russian, but also included general reflections concerning poetry and art" (*Sasha Sokolov*). In a review with Kira Sapgir, Sokolov stated the following: "“I believed that the work of a journalist would lead me faster to real prose. And since you can write more freely not in the central newspaper, but in a peripheral one, I switched to the correspondence department and left for the Mari Republic. I worked in a district newspaper, in a village, a hundred kilometers from Yoshkar-Ola. I was 22 years old. My appearance there — "a man from the capital" — was somewhat stunning. As a result, I wasn't bothered, and I could write whatever I wanted, I could even afford to experiment. I wrote mainly essays about people: I took the surname, first name, and patronymic of a person, and invented his whole life. These were, in fact, stories, and the hero could be a gamekeeper, forester, innkeeper, anyone. These were short story-essays written in rhythmic prose: if you like, close to the style of Andrei Bely, although at that time I hadn't read anything about him or his work itself. The first time I read Bely was here, abroad, and I was surprised: it looks similar" ("V 'Russkoi mysli'" 11).

text: Diminutive form of берёза. Birch. A tree type crucial to Russian culture. As Mikhail Epstein notes, "In the poem ‘Motherland' Lermontov fixes a more general meaning for the birch: it becomes one of the symbols of Russia as a whole. It is in this quality — as a 'Russian tree' — that the birch begins to be perceived as the national consciousness develops. [...] The development of that poetic motif is connected with homesickness by many poets [...]. For many poets, the birch with its bent branches, called 'weeping,' symbolizes bitterness and suffering [...]. If the birch appeared only in a weeping form, it would differ little from the willow. But the birch has another emotional and symbolic significance, a great, jubilant one. In ancient pagan rites, the birch often served as a 'May tree' (just like the spruce is a 'December' or 'New Year tree') [...]. These rites were maiden rites, men were not allowed to participate in them. [...] Birch trees were often dressed in a maiden's clothes: they wore a blouse, skirt, apron, headscarf or kokoshnik, and people called such a braided tree 'maiden's beauty.' [...] This humanization, feminization of the image of the birch [...] reaches full development and realism of details in the works of Yesenin. If the maple is the hero of his 'wood novel,' the birch is its heroine. [...] After Yesenin, the birch entered widely into the lyrical repertoire of Soviet poets" (57-61). Plant motif.

Уменьшительная форма слова "береза". Дерево, имеющее ключевое значение в русской культуре. Изображено ниже: ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/Betula_pendula_001.jpg)
Как отмечает М. Эпштейн: "В стихотворении «Родина» Лермонтов закрепляет за березой более общий смысл — одного из символов всей России. Именно в таком качестве — как "русское дерево" — и начинает восприниматься береза по мере раз вития национального самосознания […] С тоской по родине у многих поэтов связано развитие этого поэтического мотива […] У многих поэтов береза с ее склоненными ветвями, названная «плакучей», олицетворяет горечь и страдание […]. Если бы береза выступала только в плакучем облике, она мало бы отличалась от ивы. Но в березе есть и дру гая эмоциональная и символическая значимость — ве сенняя, ликующая. В древних языческих обрядах береза часто служила "майским деревом" (подобно тому, как ель — "декабрьским", "новогодним") […] Обряды эти были девичьими, мужчины к ним не допускались. […] Березку часто рядили в девичье платье: надевали кофту, юбку, фартук, на голову платок или кокошник,— и называли такое заплетенное дерево "девичьей красой". […] Это очеловечивание, "оженствление" облика березы […] в творчестве Есенина достигает полного развития и реализма подробностей. Если клен — герой его "растительного романа", то береза — героиня.  […] После Есенина береза широко вошла в лирический репертуар советских поэтов" (Epstein 57-61). Мотив растений.

text: A reference to the the Wandering Jew, whose name is said to be Ahasuerus. There are various versions of his story, but what is most relevant here are his alleged profession (shoemaker) and sin (taunting Jesus on the path to the crucifixion). The name may also conceal a reference to the nineteenth-century poet Afanasy Fet. In [Sokolov's essay on Velimir Khlebnikov](https://www.svoboda.org/a/25161164.html), he calls the Futurist poet Agasfer. When Ivan Podshivalov brings up Klebnikov in an interview, Sokolov responds: "But you see, phonetics is the yeast, the fermenting agent of language. I start with a sound; sound is like a grain from which everything else grows. It's impossible to speak about phonetics separately from meaning. [...] It takes several years of preparation to understand Khlebnikov, but it is well worth it. After Khlebnikov, Sokolov will be easy" (Podshivalov, "A Conversation" 357–358).
