text: Emblematic of paradise. There is a [Meadow Saturday located off the Irtysh River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). A reference to Gennady Karpunin's 1975 *Meadow Saturday, or, The Believable and Unbelieable Adventures of Vasya Morkovkin*. This book, a sort of modern fable, is the only one addressed to children written by the Siberian poet and literary critic Gennady Karpunin (1939-1998), famous for his works devoted to *The Tale of Igor's Campaign*. The story, full of curious characters such as its hero Vasya, concentrates on the theme of nature, whose beauty must be preserved by humans, and it addresses issues of scientific and technological progress (placed in the Soviet context) and its interaction with nature and human beings. Karpunin’s education as physicist emerges in the scientific humor contained in the book. A character in the novel defines Meadow Saturday as follows: "It's a major holiday of flowers and grass, a honey-harvest day. Do you hear bumblebees and bees buzzing? That means the clover has bloomed. Honey collected on this day is the best. It will cure any cold. This is the day of flood-meadows, the celebration of pastures. Take a look at the modest shepherd's purse growing along the roadside, even it blooms on this wonderful day. This is a day of warm earth, fragrant chernozem, a field road, and a ringing lark. That's what a Meadow Saturday is!" Read the original [here](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).
ru_trans: Олицетворение рая. Неподалеку от реки Иртыш находится деревня [Луговая Суббота](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). Отсылка к книге для детей "Луговая суббота, или Вероятные невероятные приключения Васи Морковкина", написанной Г. Карпуниным в 1975 г. Эта книга (своего рода современная басня) — единственное произведение Карпунина, адресованное детям. Г. Карпунин (1939-1998) — литературный критик и поэт, знаменитый работами о "Слове о полку Игореве". Повесть, полная любопытных персонажей, таких как ее протагонист Вася, сосредоточен на теме природы, красоту которой человек обязан беречь, и также затрагивает проблемы научно-технического прогресса (в советском контексте) и его взаимодействия с природой и человеком. Радиотехническое образование Карпунина отображается в научном юморе, присущим книге. Один из героев повести характеризует Луговую Субботу следующим образом: "О, большой праздник! Вы, молодые, не знаете его, а это очень большой праздник цветов и травы, день медосбора. Слышите, как гудят шмели и пчелы? Значит, зацвел клевер. Мед, собранный в этот день, — самый лучший, он любую простуду снимет. Это день заливных лугов, торжество пастбищ. Взгляните на скромную пастушью сумку, растущую вдоль обочины, даже она цветет в этот замечательный день. Это день теплой земли, благоуханного чернозема, полевой дороги и звенящего жаворонка. Вот какой это день Луговая суббота!". С книгой в полном объеме можно ознакомиться [здесь](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).  Мотив растений.

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой романа *Между собакой и волком* и автор того, что он называет *Заитильщиной* — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на [Приволжье](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе  (Johnson “Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition*” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (Johnson “Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Throughout the novel, geese are associated with sexual arousal. Here, they are linked to the Dama's appearance in the hunters' company. Although today far more commonly considered silly or stupid, geese have a lofty mythology. The goose has been traditional viewed as “an erotic symbol for both sexes, because it was the bird of creation, whether in the male solar form of the gods or the female lunar form of the mother goddesses" (Rowland, *Birds* 68). Similar connections between geese, sexuality, and foolishness appear elsewhere in the novel (R210, 221/E106, 125). Animal-human motif.
ru_trans: На протяжении романа, гуси ассоциируются с сексуальным возбуждением. Здесь, они связаны с появлением Дамы в компании охотников. Несмотря на современное восприятие гусей как глупых существ, мифологическая история этих птиц весьма благородна. Гуси традиционно воспринимались как "эротический символ обоих полов, будь то в форме солнца, олицетворяющего мужских богов, или луны, олицетворяющей богинь-матерей" (Rowland 68). Подобные связи между гусями, сексуальностью и глупостью встречаются далее в романе (R210, 221/E106, 125).

text: The pre-revolutionary term for the Mari peoples. The Mari live along the Volga and Kama Rivers and in the Mari El, Bashkortostan, and Tatarstan Republics. Martina Napolitano writes, "In 1968 Sokolov eventually chose to register as a non-attending student (*zaochnoe obuchenie*) due to his frustration with city life. He moved to the village of Morki in the Mari Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic with Taisiia Suvorova, a fellow student and his first wife until 1974. He then concluded his studies in 1971, having already started to collaborate with the prestigious “Literaturnaia gazeta” mainly submitting book and art reviews. His last article published on the pages of this weekly magazine, titled *Poznat' prirodu tetivy* (Knowing the nature of the bowstring), was dedicated to Mari poets. In this text, Sokolov expressed his appreciation for the first translations that appeared in Russian, but also included general reflections concerning poetry and art" (*Sasha Sokolov*). In a review with Kira Sapgir, Sokolov stated the following: "“I believed that the work of a journalist would lead me faster to real prose. And since you can write more freely not in the central newspaper, but in a peripheral one, I switched to the correspondence department and left for the Mari Republic. I worked in a district newspaper, in a village, a hundred kilometers from Yoshkar-Ola. I was 22 years old. My appearance there — "a man from the capital" — was somewhat stunning. As a result, I wasn't bothered, and I could write whatever I wanted, I could even afford to experiment. I wrote mainly essays about people: I took the surname, first name, and patronymic of a person, and invented his whole life. These were, in fact, stories, and the hero could be a gamekeeper, forester, innkeeper, anyone. These were short story-essays written in rhythmic prose: if you like, close to the style of Andrei Bely, although at that time I hadn't read anything about him or his work itself. The first time I read Bely was here, abroad, and I was surprised: it looks similar" ("V 'Russkoi mysli'" 11).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Emblematic of paradise. There is a [Meadow Saturday located off the Irtysh River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). A reference to Gennady Karpunin's 1975 *Meadow Saturday, or, The Believable and Unbelieable Adventures of Vasya Morkovkin*. This book, a sort of modern fable, is the only one addressed to children written by the Siberian poet and literary critic Gennady Karpunin (1939-1998), famous for his works devoted to *The Tale of Igor's Campaign*. The story, full of curious characters such as its hero Vasya, concentrates on the theme of nature, whose beauty must be preserved by humans, and it addresses issues of scientific and technological progress (placed in the Soviet context) and its interaction with nature and human beings. Karpunin’s education as physicist emerges in the scientific humor contained in the book. A character in the novel defines Meadow Saturday as follows: "It's a major holiday of flowers and grass, a honey-harvest day. Do you hear bumblebees and bees buzzing? That means the clover has bloomed. Honey collected on this day is the best. It will cure any cold. This is the day of flood-meadows, the celebration of pastures. Take a look at the modest shepherd's purse growing along the roadside, even it blooms on this wonderful day. This is a day of warm earth, fragrant chernozem, a field road, and a ringing lark. That's what a Meadow Saturday is!" Read the original [here](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).
ru_trans: Олицетворение рая. Неподалеку от реки Иртыш находится деревня [Луговая Суббота](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). Отсылка к книге для детей "Луговая суббота, или Вероятные невероятные приключения Васи Морковкина", написанной Г. Карпуниным в 1975 г. Эта книга (своего рода современная басня) — единственное произведение Карпунина, адресованное детям. Г. Карпунин (1939-1998) — литературный критик и поэт, знаменитый работами о "Слове о полку Игореве". Повесть, полная любопытных персонажей, таких как ее протагонист Вася, сосредоточен на теме природы, красоту которой человек обязан беречь, и также затрагивает проблемы научно-технического прогресса (в советском контексте) и его взаимодействия с природой и человеком. Радиотехническое образование Карпунина отображается в научном юморе, присущим книге. Один из героев повести характеризует Луговую Субботу следующим образом: "О, большой праздник! Вы, молодые, не знаете его, а это очень большой праздник цветов и травы, день медосбора. Слышите, как гудят шмели и пчелы? Значит, зацвел клевер. Мед, собранный в этот день, — самый лучший, он любую простуду снимет. Это день заливных лугов, торжество пастбищ. Взгляните на скромную пастушью сумку, растущую вдоль обочины, даже она цветет в этот замечательный день. Это день теплой земли, благоуханного чернозема, полевой дороги и звенящего жаворонка. Вот какой это день Луговая суббота!". С книгой в полном объеме можно ознакомиться [здесь](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).  Мотив растений.

text: Sokolov explains: "Yemelyan explains to Ilya that he, serving as a deputy, is not obliged to take a ticket, and if he sometimes takes a ticket, it is a special one, which can be used in any direction, since the route is not indicated on it. That is, it is not Ilya who takes the special ticket, but the deputy, Yemelyan. He goes on to say that he receives a sleeping berth together with the special ticket, a document which entitles him to a berth in a railcar. In addition, the deputy receives a coupon for bed linen, which is provided by the train conductor. In retelling Yemelyan's explanation, Ilya romanticizes the situation. He imagines that the sleeping car is fluttering in the wind, and the coupon is rustling. That's the kind of man he is: a poet, a fantasizer, he is prone to all kinds of beautiful things" (personal communication, June 27 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "Емельян объясняет Илье, что он, служащий попечителем, билетов брать не обязан, а если иногда билет берет, то литерный, по которому можно поехать в любом направлении, поскольку маршрут в нем не указан. То есть литерный билет берет не Илья, а попечитель Емельян. Далее он говорит, что вместе с литерным билетом он получает купейную плацкарту, то есть документ, бумагу, которая дает ему право на спальное место в купированном вагоне. Кроме того, попечитель получает талон на получение постельного белья, которое выдает проводник. Пересказывая объяснение Емельяна, Илья романтизирует ситуацию. Он воображает, что плацкарта бьется на ветру, а талон шелестит. Такой уж он человек: поэт, фантазер, он склонен к разного рода красивостям" (личная переписка, 27 июня 2023).

text: Braid, scythe, or sandback/spit. The ambiguity of the word “kosa” has a famous literary “predecessor” in Aleksandr Blok’s drama *Balaganchik* (*The Puppet Show*, 1906). The female character of Columbine has a “kosa” behind her back: either a hair braid or a scythe. The “mystics” warn Pierrot about her being Death, but he calls her his bride (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”; I don't listen to fairy tales. I am a simple man. You will not deceive me. This is Columbine. This is my bride). The ambiguity is also stressed by the character of the Author who enters the scene and exclaims: “Я не признаю [...] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” (I do not recognize [...] such allegorical wordplay: it is indecent to call a woman's braid a scythe of death! It denigrates a lady's status!). In the end, Pierrot sadly discovers that this Columbine was just a “cardboard bride” (Она картонной невестой была). The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). Read the original by Blok [here](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B8%D0%BA_(%D0%91%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%BA)).
ru_trans: Плетеная коса (прическа), серп (жнеца смерти) или речная коса. Неоднозначность слова "коса" предшествуется драмой А. А. Блока "Балаганчик" ("Шоу марионеток" 1906). У героини по имени Колумбина есть "коса" за спиной: это или плетеные волосы, или же серп. "Мистики" предупреждают Пьера о том, что Колумбина есть Смерть, но от отрицает это, называя её свой невестой (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”). Неоднозначность усиливается, когда герой Автора вторгается в сцену и восклицает: Я не признаю […] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” В конце Пьер с горестью обнаруживает, что всё это время Колубмина была "картонной невестой". Ключевая тема, связывающая женскую любовь со смертью, проводит параллель между соколовским романом и блоковским "Балаганчиком", хоть она и разрабатывалась продолжительной литературной традицией в течение очень долгого времени (например, Эрос и Танатос, "Ненавижу и люблю" Катулла). Прочитать драму Блока можно [по ссылке](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Балаганчик_(Блок)).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by  the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Warm boots for cold climates that reach the knee and lack laces. Often used in hunting. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: As Boguslawski translates it, "side-warmer," meaning a shift in weather that will warm your sides. A reference to St. Sidor Bokogrei, whose day is celebrated on May 14/27. He was given this name, because it was said that bitterly cold northern winds would stop blowing on this date. Likewise, swifts and swallows would fly to Sidor with the approach of warm weather. However, people caution against taking the appearance of the first bird as a sure sign of the cold's departure, similar to the following clause. Read his saint's life [here](https://religion.wikireading.ru/100944). The addressee of Ilya's letter is, of course, Sidor Fomich Pozhilykh. Animal motif.

text: The name Emeli'an (Emil) is derived from the Latin *aemulus* which means rival, literally "emulator." In this context, it's a fitting name given the relationship between Ilya and his brother, as well as the fluid nature of the divisions between characters' identities. Aemilianus was also briefly Roman emperor in 253. Ostanin notes that Emel'yan was also the name of Pugachev, a Cossack ataman who led a popular insurrection during the reign of Catherine the Great (52). His figure turned literary thanks to Pushkin and his historical novel *The Captain's Daughter* (1836). In Pushkin’s novel, Pugachev is described through the eyes of the nobleman Grinev who dislikes this illiterate “drunkard” wandering outlaw, yet does not refuse him his hareskin coat as a token of his gratitude. During the first Russo-Turkish war (1768–1774) Pugachev served in the Russian army as *khorunzhy*, a military rank mentioned in chapter 3.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: A tree type crucial to Russian culture. As Mikhail Epstein notes, "In the poem ‘Motherland' Lermontov fixes a more general meaning for the birch: it becomes one of the symbols of Russia as a whole. It is in this quality – as a 'Russian tree' – that the birch begins to be perceived as the national consciousness develops. [...] The development of that poetic motif is connected with homesickness by many poets [...]. For many poets, the birch with its bent branches, called 'weeping,' symbolizes bitterness and suffering [...]. If the birch appeared only in a weeping form, it would differ little from the willow. But the birch has another emotional and symbolic significance, a great, jubilant one. In ancient pagan rites, the birch often served as a 'May tree' (just like the spruce is a 'December' or 'New Year tree') [...]. These rites were maiden rites, men were not allowed to participate in them. [...] Birch trees were often dressed in a maiden's clothes: they wore a blouse, skirt, apron, headscarf or kokoshnik, and people called such a braided tree 'maiden's beauty.' [...] This humanization, feminization of the image of the birch [...] reaches full development and realism of details in the works of Yesenin. If the maple is the hero of his 'wood novel,' the birch is its heroine. [...] After Yesenin, the birch entered widely into the lyrical repertoire of Soviet poets" (57–61). Plant motif.

text: Here, the Finist substitutes for the common pigeon. See the fairy tale "The Feather of Finist the Falcon" (or "Finist the Falcon") collected by Aleksandr Afanas'yev. text: Foma Pogibel' is one of the two oarsmen who carry people (dead or alive) across the river (a variation of the Charon Greek myth). The other oarsman is Eryoma (diminutive of Eremei, Jeremiah). However, in Note XXXI the oarsman is called Pavel, just like the character who sends his uncle Pyotr to get yeast in Gorodnishche. As underlined by one of the epigraphs in Sokolov’s first novel, *A School for Fools*, the biblical name of Pavel is somehow interchangeable: “Saul, who is called Paul” (see [Acts 13:9–10](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts+13%3A9-10&version=NIV;NRT)). As for Foma, he carries a biblical name, too (Thomas), whose Aramaic origin suggests the idea of the “twin.” This apostle is famous as “Doubting Thomas” due to his denial of the resurrection of Jesus, according to the Gospel of John (see [John 20:24–31](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+20%3A24-31&version=NIV;NRT)). In the Orthodox tradition, the Sunday following Easter is called “Thomas Sunday”: the day when Christ appeared to his disciples; it took seeing Jesus’ body for Thomas to name him “My Lord and my God.”

text: Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe. In Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* Tereus is transformed into a hoopoe and searches for his missing family, calling out "where, where" in the bird's famous song. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family, but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" (Vergara, "Flap" 366). text: Mountain ash. As Mikhail Epstein notes, "This is the brightest of trees, glowing with all shades of crimson. At the same time, the mountain ash reveals that bitterness and sadness that are generally inseparable from Russian nature. Often its red berries, associated with blood, sacrifice, suffering, convey not melancholy, but audacity, challenge, fury, and rage. This motif found concentrated expression in Alexander Blok’s poem 'Autumn Will' [...]. If the birch embodies the shyness, simplicity, and dimness of Russian nature, then the mountain ash is its fiery principle. [...] However, the berries ripen in the fall, and they have a reflection of some kind of cold, withering. Hence Yesenin’s image of the mountain ash as a fire that does not burn [...] if the birch found its poet in Yesenin, then the mountain ash in Tsvetaeva [...] In Tsvetaeva, two motifs, for the most part separated earlier, seem to come together: the bitter and the fiery mountain ash [...] The mountain ash accompanies her during all her life, like the willow accompanies Akhmatova. Just as the meanings of the willow and the mountain ash are opposite in the language of trees, so are the creative systems of Akhmatova and Tsvetaeva in Russian poetry. The willow is weeping sorrow, the mountain ash is burning pain, the willow is languid, the mountain ash is impetous, the willow is tears from the eyes, the mountain ash is blood from a wound, the willow is tender, drowsy, the mountain ash is passionate, rebellious. Such is Russia, a fiery bitterness, for Tsvetaeva" (66–68, 70). Plant motif.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Egor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.

As a result, I wasn't bothered, and I could write whatever I wanted, I could even afford to experiment. I wrote mainly essays about people: I took the surname, first name, and patronymic of a person, and invented his whole life. These were, in fact, stories, and the hero could be a gamekeeper, forester, innkeeper, anyone. These were short story-essays written in rhythmic prose: if you like, close to the style of Andrei Bely, although at that time I hadn't read anything about him or his work itself. The first time I read Bely was here, abroad, and I was surprised: it looks similar" ("V Russkoi mysli" 11).

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the Zaitil'shchina, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286). Pozhilykh is transferred from one narrative level (Ilya's letter to the investigator) to another (the third-person narrator's account of Yakov's life and imagination). Furthermore, he's here inserted into this imagined scenario involving French royalty.

Maple. Plant motif. As Ostanin notes, Sokolov was born in Canada, whose official emblem is the maple leaf (113). Epshtein explains that "Unlike the oak, the maple and the poplar trees do not have such a definite, formed figurative nucleus in Russian poetry. The fact is that even in folklore traditions associated with ancient pagan rituals, these trees did not play such a significant role. Poetic visions of them are mainly formed in the twentieth century [...]. If the oak is a representative of stout vitality, it is a kind of king and a man among the trees, then the maple is a frivolous guy, a little crazy, with an exuberant pile of uncombed hair [...]. The image of the maple is most developed in the poetry of Sergei Yesenin, where it acts as a sort of lyrical hero of the 'wood novel.' The image of the maple tree as a country boy, a walker, a suitor is most clearly depicted [...]. Another stable figurative motif associated with the maple is the toothedness of its leaves, which remotely resemble the shape of a heart, making the maple as if it were the patron saint of love [...]." Here Epstein mentions in particular works by Fet, Blok, Zabolotsky, Akhmatova. “The Maple is often associated with the concept of chastity, purity. In Fet's poetry the maple is said to be ‘virgin,' in Blok's it is 'fresh,' in Pasternak's there is 'not even a speck in the new maples…’” (50–53). Plant motif.
ru_trans: Как отмечает Останин, Соколов родился в Канаде, официальный символ которой —кленовый лист (113). Эпштейн поясняет, что "в отличие от дуба, клен и другие тополи не имеют такого определенного, сформировавшегося образного ядра в русской поэзии. Дело в том, что даже в фольклорных традициях, неотрывно связанных с древними языческими ритуалами, эти деревья не играли значительной роли. Поэтические представления о них формируются в основном в XX веке [...]. Если дуб, будучи представителем крепкой жизненной силы, является своего рода королем среди деревьев, клен, в таком случает, выступает как легкомысленный и слегка сумасшедший парень с буйной копной нечесаных волос [...]. Образ клена наиболее развит в поэзии Сергея Есенина, где он становится своеобразным лирическим героем «лесного романа». Другой устоявшийся образ клена — зубчатость его листьев, отдаленно напоминающих форму его сердца, отдаленно напоминающих форму сердца; это превращает клен в некого святого покровителя любви [...]". Здесь Эпштейн упоминает, в частности, произведения Фета, Блока, Заболоцкого, Ахматовой. "Клен зачастую ассоциируется с идеей целомудрия, чистоту. В поэзии Блога клен 'девственен', у Блока — 'свеж', а у Пастернака он описывается так: 'в новых кленах нет ни пятнышка...'" (50-53). Мотив растений.

text: The mythical Firebird from Slavic folklore. Read the original [here](https://xn----7sbb5adknde1cb0dyd.xn--p1ai/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/) and an English translation [here](http://www.artrusse.ca/fairytales/firebird.htm). The story is set in a kingdom where an unknown thief is stealing apples from the king’s garden. The three princes must find out who is the thief: the younger, Ivan, observes that it is a marvelous Firebird stealing the apples, but he is only able to catch one of the bird’s feathers. The king is amazed by its beauty and orders his sons to capture the Firebird, an adventure that will be successful in the end only for Ivan. However, on his way back, he takes a rest and his brothers, out of envy, decide to kill him. Thanks to the help of a wolf friend, Ivan manages to recover and reestablish order in the kingdom. The motif of theft and the figure of the wolf (in the folk tale, a positive hero according to Vladimir Propp, famed Soviet folklorist) are relevant to Sokolov’s novel, too. Animal motif.
ru_trans: Мифическая Жар-птица из славянского фольклора. Прочитать сказку о ней можно [здесь](https://онлайн-читать.рф/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/). История разворачивается в царстве, где неизвестный крадет яблоки из королевского сада. Трем принцам нужно найти вора. Младший, Иван-царевич, замечает, что дивная Жар-птица крадет яблоки, но ему удается поймать лишь пару ее перьев. Король изумляется их красотой и поручает сыновьям захватить Жар-птицу, в чем, в конце концов, преуспеет лишь Иван-царевич. Однако на пути назад он решает отдохнуть, и, преисполненные завистью, братья решают убить его. С помощью друга-волка у Ивана-царевича удается вернуться и восстановить порядок в царстве. Мотив воровства и фигура волка (в фольклоре являющемуся положительным персонажем, согласно известному совесткому фольклористу Владимиру Проппу) не чужды и роману Соколова. Жар-птица также является в названии Записки 27 (R239/E156). Как следует из метафоры в конце стихотворения, под Жар-птицей может подразумеваться алкоголь. Мотив животных. Тема алкоголя.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). Его альтернативно называют Федором и Егором: выбор, судя по всему, обусловлен наличием гласных "е/ё" и "о". Имя Петр в переводе с греческого означает "камень". Апостол Петр (Симон Петр), по происхождению рыбак, считается первым христианским Папой. Петр трижды отрекся от Иисуса во время событий распятия, как и предсказывал Иисус (см. [от Матфея 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69–75&version=NIV;NRT)). Федор (Феодор) означает "Божий дар". Имя Егор — вариация имени Георгий (Георгий), от греческого "земледелец". Он был увековечен как святой в легенде о Драконе (Святом Георгии Драконоборце). В главе 10 этому герою бросают вызов повеситься, что приводит к его самоубийству.

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
