In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Alexander Boguslawski notes that variations on this word are used in four key moments in the novel (R155, 157, 225, 254/E12, 14–15, 132, 185) and that the "close parallels between the first and last use of the phrase should be noted — this is the frame within which two other versions of the expression exist. These two framing elements are built around the word *nevterpezh*, a colloquial adverb, usually used after a noun or pronoun in dative case and often with auxiliary verbs to be or to become. Thus, the expression "mne stalo nevterpezh" [it became unbearable to me; I could not stand it any longer], [sic] is common. However, Sokolov makes some important alterations to the expression — first, he discards the dative government and substitutes another verb for the auxiliary" ("How Sokolov's" 218).

text: Olga Matich reads Sokolov's novel as an extended response to Boris Pilnyak's short story "Mother Earth" (1927), as it shares confusion between a wolf and a fox, a character name Arina, and a setting on the Upper Volga, among other similarities ("Sasha Sokolov" 312–313). Read the original [here](http://az.lib.ru/p/pilxnjak_b_a/text_1924_mat_syra_zemlya.shtml). D. Barton Johnson adds: "The prose models that served for *Shkola dlia durakov* were obviously unsuitable for the setting and events of *Mezhdu sobakoi i volkom*. Apart from the obvious sections of literary parody in which Gogol' is flagrantly apparent, it is difficult to point to direct stylistic sources. The first that comes to mind is the Andrei Belyi of *Serebrianyi golub*' (*The Silver Dove*) with its (partial) peasant setting and its elaborate sound instrumentation. Sokolov, however, denies having read Belyi at this point. A more likely literary context is afforded by modernist Boris Pilniak […] Pilniak had recently been rehabilitated and his work was easily available. Sokolov recalls reading his work in 1975. Something of the same dark violence and fractured language is also to be found in the work of Pilniak's adherent Andrei Platonov whose work was being rediscovered and republished in the late 1960s" ("Background Notes" (336–337).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

Diminutive form of Orina. Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

ru_trans: Уменьшительная форма имени "Орина". Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the Zaitil'shchina, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: A name given to blind wanderers who sing spiritual poems. Originally, the word did not refer to disabled or crippled beggars, as it does now, but rather to wanderers who visited holy places and sang songs. The term is derived from the Latin *caligae*, Since these wanderers often lived off of alms in the towns they visited (and occasionally settled in), the term took on the meaning of a disabled person who does the same in its modern usage. ([Miller 27–28](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%AD%D0%A1%D0%91%D0%95/%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B8_%D0%B8%D0%BB%D0%B8_%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D0%B8_%D0%BF%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%B5)) Also mentioned in chapter 8 (R209/E103), chapter 9 (R214/E112), and chapter 10 (R223/E129). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
ru_trans: Так прозвали странников, поющих духовные песни. Изначально слово не применялось к людям с инвалидностью или покалеченным попрошайкам, будучи, напротив, термином, определявших странников, совершавших хождения к святым местам и певшим песни. Термин происходит от латинского слова *caligae*. Поскольку эти странники зачастую жили за счет милостыни в городах, в которых они блуждали (и где иногда даже селились), в современном употреблении этот термин приобрел значение инвалида, который делает то же самое (Miller 27–28). Также упоминается в главах 8 (R209/E103), 9 (R214/E112) и 10 (R223/E129). Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает более двадцати видов обуви, встречающихся в трех романах Соколова: “башмаки, ботфорты, боты, ботинки (полуботинки), чеботы, чизмы, чубуры, галоши (калоши), геты, ичиги, кеды, клоги, лапти, мокроступы, обуви (обувки), сапоги, сандалии, тапочки (полутапочки), шлепанцы, штиблеты, тапти, туфли, валенки. В интервью с А. и Н. Воронелями, Соколов называет Бунина и Гоголя своими “современниками, сотрудниками по цеху, старшими мастерами” (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Мотив обуви.

text: Vasily Karaban appears as the messenger who brings news of the phenomenon of Orina in the form of Everlastin’ Life or that Dame to the Volga community in which the novel is set. He is her first victim and, while he remains alive, he has shriveled up. His occupation, as Sokolov confirms, is unclear (personal communication, July 7, 2023). The name Karaban is of Turkic origin and can either be a surname or a nickname, a shortened version of Karabanov. It means “black mole” from “kara” (black) and “ban” (mole, birthmark). According to Turkic folklore, a black mole is a sign of happiness. Therefore, in the context of *Between Dog and Wolf*, it may be an ironic marker given Karaban’s fate ("Proiskhozhdenie familii Karabanova”).

text: Diminutive form of Orina. Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). Paklia and paklina are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья здесь обращается к себе в третьем лице. Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

Подобные поселения, свободные от повинностей, были упразднены в начале XVIII века и стали обыкновенными деревнями. Зачастую, пригородные районы поглощались близлежащими городами. В современном языке, "слобода" в разных областях относится к населенному пункту в сельской местности. Соколов подтверждет, что [слобода](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) может быть найдена у [реки Волга](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) в Конаковском районе (личная переписка, 7 июня 2023).

text: Ostanin has identified this phrase as a borrowing from the 1945 drinking song "The Lonely Button Accordion" ("Одинокая гармонь") by Mikhail Isakovsky. The song tells the story of a wandering accordion player who keeps girls awak at night with his music. One of the lines, "young accordion player" (гармонист молодой) echoes *Between Dog and Wolf*'s second epigraph: "The young man was a hunter" (Молодой человек был охотник). Read the lyrics (in Russian) [here](https://drinking-songs.ru/slova-pesen/odinokaya-garmon.html). Listen to a recording [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KJYBZwpZc_c).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах ("Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the Zaitil'shchina, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). Shimmering through its portrayal of the desolate state of humanity, its images of frozen river and skating, the ekphrasis re-emerges in Il'ia's 'allegory' of existence: in what appears to be an elaboration of Auden’s dogs that ‘go on with their doggy life'" (*The Prose* 63).

text: Diminutive form of Orina. Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time […]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama, ta devochka, ta bobylka, ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). Paklia and paklina are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

Archaism for объедение: gluttony, a delight to eat, something incredibly delicious. This form encodes the word for poison (яд), creating a link between Ilya's lusting after Orina, his tastes, and death. Along with the various drinking allusions in this section, a reference to [Luke 21:34](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+21%3A34&version=NIV): "Be careful, or your hearts will be weighed down with carousing, drunkenness and the anxieties of life, and that day will close on you suddenly like a trap."

text: Dancing. This word is crucial to Sokolov's art. Chorea — a movement disorder belonging to the dyskinesias group of neurological disorders. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek "χορεία" and was used to described the movements of those inflicted by the disease. Sokolov's first novel, *A School for Fools*, is dedicated to Vitia Pliaskin, which refers to Sydenham's chorea (also known as "St. Vitus's dance, пляска святого Вита in Russian). Watch a video [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTCnbga3sqg). Referred to several times in the novel (R171, 191, 205, 214, 215/E37, 74, 97, 113, 115).

It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of ta dama's victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен (*paklen*) and неклен (*neklen*) are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Neklina, Paklina). As Sokolov explains, “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, “Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (Johnson, “Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Ilya wishes (possibly ironically) to understand what is the sense, the meaning of such a fairy tale, whether it is a parable carrying any meaning at all, or not. In a sense, this is what the reader may wonder reading Sokolov's novel and failing to grasp its plot, structure, and levels of interpretation. Possibly, this is a (Nabokovian) provocation for readers who search for meaning in any literary work. Before agreeing to appear in [Maxim Gureev's documentary film](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8RoUlCN2yxk) about him, Sokolov asked the director whether he had a script prepared. When Gureev replied in the negative, Sokolov responded positively: "Plot... That side of literature never appealed to me. Plot is a contrived thing. Plot is used to sell something. For me it's important how language works, the linguistic dance of its own kind. If I was born in a different time, in a different place, in a different family, I would have become a composer, because language is one of the forms of music" (Gureev 165–166).
ru_trans: Илья хочет (возможно, иронически) понять, в чем смысл, значение такой сказки, является ли она несущей в себе хоть какой-то смысл притчей или нет. В каком-то смысле, тем же вопросом задается и читатель, читающий роман Соколова и не понимающий его сюжета, структуры и уровней интерпретации. Возможно, это (набоковская) провокация для читателей, которые ищут смысл в любом литературном произведении. Прежде чем согласиться сняться в [документальном фильме Максима Гуреева](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8RoUlCN2yxk), Соколов спросил у режиссера, есть ли у него подготовленный сценарий. Когда Гуреев ответил отрицательно, Соколов ответил положительно: "Сюжет — меня эта сторона литературы никогда не увлекала. Сюжет — это надуманная вещь, сюжет — это на продажу. Для меня важно, как работает язык, этот своего рода лингвистический танец. Если бы я родился в другое время, в другом месте, в другой семье, я стал бы композитором, потому что язык одна из форм музыки" (Gureev 165-166).
