text: An important parable is contained in the fifth chapter of Sokolov’s first novel, *A School for Fools*, and is entitled “The Carpenter in the Desert.” According to many scholars, this text represents a key moment not only within the plot of this specific novel but for Sokolov’s art in general: Ludmilla Litus affirms that “this parable [...] provides an important clue to understanding the work as a whole” (“Aesopian Language” 129); Leiderman and Lipovetksy write that “the central episode of this chapter, Saul's parable of the carpenter [...] is important above all because it metamorphoses categories that previously belonged to the polar worldviews presented in *A School for Fools*: creator and executioner, bird and victim, executioner and victim. Creator — executioner — bird — victim form here a certain undivided flowing whole” (*Russkaia literatura dvadtsatogo veka* 406); Margaret Ziolkowski notices that “like a biblical parable, [...] it asserts that corruption constitutes self-betrayal and that a dedication to lofty aesthetic aims does not afford protection against surrender to crass temptation [...]. his avian guise provides a vision of the carpenter's true spiritual essence” (411). Mario Caramitti in his doctoral dissertation explains that through this parable “Sokolov expresses his theory of art in the most complete manner. Sokolov's carpenter, after briefly transforming into a bird, kills himself by volunteering to crucify another carpenter, in exchange for the tools he needs to continue working. In essence, master and prophet annihilate each other in the presence of insurmountable impediments external to art. If we then consider that in *Palisandriia* there is even a 'назаретский плотник' (a carpenter from Nazareth), the field of ambivalence comes to fully involve not only the inspired artist and the craftsman, but also the divine and the human, co-present and conflicting. The artist, like Christ, is both God and man, he is both victim and executioner of himself, and like Christ he is the absolute arbiter of his own destiny, the master and responsible for his own art, whatever the external circumstances that influence him. The artistic vocation reconfirms itself as an energy that is difficult to control and has disturbing implications. The carpenter protests, 'Но я мастер, а не палач' (But I’m a master craftsman and not an executioner). But blind faith in the art nonetheless leads him to the execrable choice: 'Ты ведь – плотник, а плотник обязан забивать гвозди, это дело его жизни' (You’re a carpenter and carpenters are supposed to hammer nails, it’s their mission in life). The role in the parable played by the men who in exchange for wood and nails ask the carpenter to crucify himself (through his fellow man) remains to be defined. On the one hand, one might tend to associate them with the no less ambiguous Those Who Came of the first chapter of the novel, thus keeping them in the realm of personal mythology. On the other hand, as Ludmila Litus (“Aesopian Language” 128–132) shows with discreetly convincing arguments, they could be emissaries of the totalitarian society, which allows the artist to work only if they accept the compromise. In this case, given the desert setting, the association with diabolic temptation would also be immediate” (“Strategie” 153).

Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: A reference to the expression “У сороки боли, у вороны боли, а у (имя) всё заживи” ("The magpie is hurt, the crow is hurt, but (name) will feel all better"), used to comfort children who have hurt themselves. According to Edward Armstrong’s *The Folklore of Birds*, “magpie lore seems to be dependent upon, or derive from, raven traditions to a considerable extent and the folklore of the crow is confused with that of the raven" (72). Crows, like ravens, are often associated with death (Armstrong 75). José Vergara writes, "As for the crow, so consistently paired with the magpie, there is the story of Coronis, whose adultery is revealed by a tattling crow. After Apollo condemns her to death, he feels remorse and turns the crow’s white feathers black as punishment. Here, again, we note the theme of transformations and the unfaithful woman, who, in the form of Orina, would make the crow Ilya" ("Flap 369). Animal motif.

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the Zaitil'shchina, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). text: Vasily Karaban appears as the messenger who brings news of the phenomenon of Orina in the form of Everlastin’ Life or that Dame to the Volga community in which the novel is set. He is her first victim and, while he remains alive, he has shriveled up. His occupation, as Sokolov confirms, is unclear (personal communication, July 7, 2023). The name Karaban is of Turkic origin and can either be a surname or a nickname, a shortened version of Karabanov. It means “black mole” from “kara” (black) and “ban” (mole, birthmark). According to Turkic folklore, a black mole is a sign of happiness. Therefore, in the context of Between Dog and Wolf, it may be an ironic marker given Karaban’s fate ("Proiskhozhdenie familii Karabanova”).

text: Although appearing only now, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the only fictional author of the entire book.  In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is “not fresh and not young”); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov plays a central role also in the structuring of the plot, as it is him who kills Ilya in revenge.

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic suggests Ilya is his father. Yet, the suggestion is debatable. D.B. Johnson noted: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (...). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (1984; 211-212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and kills it. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья здесь обращается к себе в третьем лице. Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он — юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Ilya returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

Тем не менее, и Яков, и Илья не имеют ни малейшего подозрения об этом, и когда их дальнейшие жизни в качестве точильщика и собаковода окончательно и бесповортно пересекаются, они в равной степени и не знают о своей скоротечной дружбе в больнице (…). Соколов переосмыслил и инсценировал греческую трагедию об Эдипе в верховьях Волги" (“Sasha Sokolov's 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). Действительно, Илья будет убит Яковым в качестве отомщения за то, что первый (в сумерках, пересекая замороженную реку) ошибочно принимает одну из собак последнего за волка и убивает ее. После того, как охотник крадет его костыли, Илья возвращается, чтобы убить собак. Для более подробного ознакомления с мифопоэтикой Соколова см. работу И. В. text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Pine tree. As Mikhail Epstein notes, "Pines and spruce trees represent part of a gloomy, harsh landscape; wilderness, darkness, and silence reign around them. [...] Pines and spruces mean not only the peace of sleep, but also the peace of death. If an oak tree that has grown over a grave is a symbol of eternal life overcoming death, then the pine tree is perceived as a tombstone erected by nature itself over a person and confirming the hopelessness of death […]. The pine tree stands out for its slenderness and height, which allows it to “converse” with the wind. One of the most persistent poetic motifs is pine trees swayed by the wind like bells, causing a ringing sound throughout the forest [...]. The slenderness of pine trunks gives reason to compare them with columns and strings" (75–76, 80). Plant motif.

text: Sokolov has written about his desire to avoid the "what" in literature," opting for the "how": “In the milieu from which I come […] the traditions of so-called art-for-art’s sake are still alive. I am using here the expression so-called because by definition art is always for its own sake […] Forgive me for being so insistent, but art should be beautiful. And prose – should be refined and superior like poetry. […] Show me your how – a pass to truth, and take away what; I will find what myself.” (Sokolov, “The Key Word of Belles-Lettres,” *In the House of the Hanged*, 28-29).

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Animal-human motif.

text: Ilya here refers to himself in the third person. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья здесь обращается к себе в третьем лице. Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как “полуграмотный бред”, удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (“Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf and the Modernist Tradition” 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что “егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Ilya's fascination with Meadow Saturday (above). Emblematic of paradise. There is a [Meadow Saturday located off the Irtysh River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). A reference to Gennady Karpunin's 1975 *Meadow Saturday, or, The Believable and Unbelieable Adventures of Vasya Morkovkin*. This book, a sort of modern fable, is the only one addressed to children written by the Siberian poet and literary critic Gennady Karpunin (1939-1998), famous for his works devoted to *The Tale of Igor's Campaign*. The story, full of curious characters such as its hero Vasya, concentrates on the theme of nature, whose beauty must be preserved by humans, and it addresses issues of scientific and technological progress (placed in the Soviet context) and its interaction with nature and human beings. Karpunin’s education as physicist emerges in the scientific humor contained in the book. A character in the novel defines Meadow Saturday as follows: "It's a major holiday of flowers and grass, a honey-harvest day. Do you hear bumblebees and bees buzzing? That means the clover has bloomed. Honey collected on this day is the best. It will cure any cold. This is the day of flood-meadows, the celebration of pastures. Take a look at the modest shepherd's purse growing along the roadside, even it blooms on this wonderful day. This is a day of warm earth, fragrant chernozem, a field road, and a ringing lark. That's what a Meadow Saturday is!" Read the original [here](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).
ru_trans: Илья заворожен с вышеупомянутой Луговой Субботой, что являет из себя олицетворение рая. Неподалеку от реки Иртыш находится деревня [Луговая Суббота](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Lugovaya+Subbota,+Tyumen+Oblast,+Russia,+626185/@59.8036429,69.7688218,10.38z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x439f7f579c2ef6a9:0x192baa4bb80bd68e!8m2!3d59.8530046!4d69.786791). Отсылка к книге для детей "Луговая суббота, или Вероятные невероятные приключения Васи Морковкина", написанной Г. Карпуниным в 1975 г. Эта книга (своего рода современная басня) — единственное произведение Карпунина, адресованное детям. Г. Карпунин (1939-1998) — литературный критик и поэт, знаменитый работами о "Слове о полку Игореве". Повесть, полная любопытных персонажей, таких как ее протагонист Вася, сосредоточен на теме природы, красоту которой человек обязан беречь, и также затрагивает проблемы научно-технического прогресса (в советском контексте) и его взаимодействия с природой и человеком. Радиотехническое образование Карпунина отображается в научном юморе, присущим книге. Один из героев повести характеризует Луговую Субботу следующим образом: "О, большой праздник! Вы, молодые, не знаете его, а это очень большой праздник цветов и травы, день медосбора. Слышите, как гудят шмели и пчелы? Значит, зацвел клевер. Мед, собранный в этот день, — самый лучший, он любую простуду снимет. Это день заливных лугов, торжество пастбищ. Взгляните на скромную пастушью сумку, растущую вдоль обочины, даже она цветет в этот замечательный день. Это день теплой земли, благоуханного чернозема, полевой дороги и звенящего жаворонка. Вот какой это день Луговая суббота!". С книгой в полном объеме можно ознакомиться [здесь](https://royallib.com/read/karpunin_gennadiy/lugovaya_subbota.html#0).  Мотив растений.

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он — юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

Список можно расширить, включив такие атрибуты, как носки, чулки, портянки, гамаши, коньки, костыли и протезы” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). В интервью с А. и Н. Воронелями, Соколов называет Бунина и Гоголя своими “современниками, сотрудниками по цеху, старшими мастерами” (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Мотив обуви.

text: Dated: February. It will be mentioned again in chapter 14 (another chapter by Ilya). The word derives from the terms "бок" (side) and "греть" (to warm). As Boguslawski translates it, "side-warmer," meaning a shift in weather that will warm your sides. A reference to St. Sidor Bokogrei, whose day is celebrated on May 14/27. He was given this name, because it was said that bitterly cold northern winds would stop blowing on this date. Likewise, swifts and swallows would fly to Sidor with the approach of warm weather. However, people caution against taking the appearance of the first bird as a sure sign of the cold's departure, similar to the following clause. Read his saint's life [here](https://religion.wikireading.ru/100944). The addressee of Ilya's letter is, of course, Sidor (Fomich Pozhilykh).

Однако не рекомендуется принимать появление первой птицы за надежный признак ухода холодов, как и следующее положение; прочитать житие святого можно [по ссылке](https://religion.wikireading.ru/100944). text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.

text: Yakov Alfeev's patronymic implies that Ilya is his father. However, this reading is debatable. D.B. Johnson notes: "Yakov is Ilya's son – to whatever extent anything is anything in the twilight world between dog and wolf. Both Yakov and Ilya remain unaware of this, however, and when their later lives as grinder and dogkeeper finally and fatally cross, they are equally unaware of their transient friendship in the hospital (…). [Yakov is] re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus. He unwittingly both kills his father and (albeit not literally) 'marries' a version of his mother. Sokolov has restaged the Greek myth of Oedipus amid the headwaters of the Volga” (“Sasha Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211–212). In fact, Ilya will be killed by Yakov in revenge, as the former (at twilight, while crossing the frozen river) takes one of the latter's dogs for a wolf and attacks it. After the hunters steal his crutches, Yakov returns to murder the dogs. For a consideration of Sokolov's mythopoetics, see also Ashcheulova's "Tvorchestvo Sashi Sokolova v kontekste literaturnogo protsessa 60-80-x godov."

text: Diminutive of Ilya. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Уменьшительная форма имени "Илья". Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: Ilya's conversation with the river here is continued in chapter 4 (R176/E47-48). There, the "Страшнеющего Суда" becomes "последнем случае." The threat of death and the pull of suicide looms over Ilya and many of the men living on the banks of the Volga. However, as Martina Napolitano explains, "As if to exorcise it, as if to disavow it as incompatible with the characters' very personal idea of a-chronological, nonlinear, circular and modifiable time, death is always spoken of in a metaphorical key" ("'Studyin This Volapuke'" 287). Death is one of Sokolov's central themes. As he put it in an interview with Olga Matich, "In that sense, I'm apparently traditional. I write on eternal themes: love, life, death. Death is inseparable from life. It's constantly near, around us, in the objects that surround us. It becomes clearer in certain of its forms. For example, in old photographs. Since I was a child I've had a thought: everyone in photos from the previous century, at the very least those born in its first half, died. This fact particularly stands out when you look at group photos, at snapshots of massive street scenes. Or when you're simply walking down the street at rush hour and suddenly see a freeze frame. All movement, the entire crowd momentarily stops, and you suddenly remember: in 60-70 years all of them will no longer be. Yourself included" ("Nuzhno zabyt'" 12). This fascination with death dates back to his childhood: "Visiting cemeteries [...] was for me something like a home education. I was also interested in the theme of death. It's, after all, the most interesting thing in life" (Kochetkova).
ru_trans: Разговор Ильи с рекой продолжается в главе 4 (R176/E47-48). Здесь, выражение "до Страшнеющего Суда" становится синонимичным "в последнем случае". Угроза смерти и тяга к самоубийству давлеет над Ильей и другими обитателями берегов Волги. Однако, как объясняет М. Наполитано: "Будто бы бы для того, чтобы освободиться, отречься от нее как от идеи, несовместимой с весьма личным ахронологическим, нелинейным, спиралевидным, легкоизменяемым понятием времени героев, о смерти всегда говорится в метафорическом ключе" (Napolitano, "'Studyin This Volapuke'" 287). Смерть является одной из центральных тем в творчестве Соколова. Как он замечает в интервью с Ольгой Матич: "В этом смысле я, видимо, традиционен. Пишу на вечные темы: любовь, жизнь, смерть. Смерть неотлучима от жизни. Она постоянно рядом, вокруг нас, в окружающих нас предметах. В некоторых из них ее облик проступает ясней. Например, в старых фотографиях. Меня с детства занимала мысль: все люди на снимках прошлого века, во всяком случае — родившиеся в первой половине его, умерли. Особенно этот факт поражает при взгляде на групповые фото, на снимки массовых уличных сцен. Или просто идешь по улице в часы пик и вдруг видишь как бы стоп-кадр: все движение, вся толпа мгновенно останавливается и вспоминаешь вдруг: через 60-70 лет их всех тоже не будет. И тебя в том числе" (Solokov, "Nuzhno zabyt'" 12). Увлечение темой смерти зародилось еще в детстве: "Посещение кладбищ — не только Ваганьковского, но и Симоновского и Новодевичьего — было для меня чем-то вроде домашнего образования. Меня тоже интересовала тема смерти — это ведь самое интересное, что есть в жизни" (Kochetkova).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).
ru_trans: Крылобыл (названный здесь через уменьшительное имя) — ключевой персонаж, обитающий в мире мертвых (живущий на другом берегу Итиля, в Выдогоще). Это неудивительно, ведь его "говорящее имя" образовано словами "крыло" и "был". Он — ипостась ангельского существа, направляющего Илью в его странствиях и наводящего его на идеи и размышления: в главе 4 именно Крылобыл выдвинул мысль о происхождении буквы "ж"; именно Крылобыла в 14 главе Илья описывает как "умнягу", который "увещает", " кому доверяю, кого хвалю". В каком-то смысле Крылобыл — это Вергилий или даже Беатриче Ильи в его странствованиях по этому особого рода Аду, Чистилищу и Раю. Ближе к концу романа рассказчик в главе 16 (R275/E220) и Илья в главе 17 будут обращаться к нему как "Федот Федоров" (R279/E227).

text: Although appearing first only in chapter 4, this polymorphic character occupies a central role in the novel, being at once a dogkeeper, a hunter, a poet, a painter, and possibly the fictional author of the entire book. The ambiguity of his character is rooted in the similarity of his name with the word якобы (allegedly, supposedly). In a reply to Smith, published in a 1987 article ("The Verse in Sasha *Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf*"), Sokolov himself stated that: "the verse chapters are written by Iakov. He has nothing to do with me, but he has to be and is 'sophisticated', because he is that same painter who is discussed in the prose chapters (not the ones from Il'ia) 'The Hunter's Tale', where he is the youth living in his mother's house; the boy in love with the simple-minded girl whom the sailors take under the boat; the sketcher, the author of the Self-Portrait in Uniform and so forth; (And, of course, here, in this chapter, he is the hunter and poet who is ‘not fresh and not young’); 'The Hunter's Tale, or Pictures from an Exhibition', where he is Iakov Il'ich Palamakhterov, 'the incorruptible witness who is journeying towards the end of his practical and pitiless time,' and imagines the scene from nineteenth-century ethnography in which his greatgrandfather takes part; 'Pictures from an Exhibition' (9), where he observes street scenes from the window of a cadet school; see also the other similar parts of the book, 13 and 16. They are written (all of them) from the point of view of an author, but that of a stylized author, i.e., once again, not directly from myself. Iakov is a poet, a painter, a dreamer, a member of the intelligentsia, who was born and grew up in the city. He is already grown up when he comes to the Itil” (327). Yakov is likewise crucial to the structuring of the plot, as it is he who kills Ilya in revenge for the latter’s attack on his dogs.
ru_trans: Несмотря на то, что появляется он только в главе 4, этот полиморфный герой играет центральную роль в произведении, одновременно будучи хозяином собаки, охотником, поэтом, художником и, возможно, вымышленным автором целой книги. В ответе на статью Дж. Смита, выпущенную в 1987 ("The Verse in Sasha Sokolov's Between Dog and Wolf"), Соколов заявил: "Главы в стихах написаны Яковом. Он не имеет ничего общего со мной, однако он должен быть и есть 'изысканный', потому что он и есть тот самый художник, о котором идет речь в прозаических главах (не тех, что написаны Ильей) 'Рассказ охотника', где он — юноша, живущий в доме своей матери; юноша, влюбленный в простодушную девушку, которую моряки берут под лодку; эскизный художник, автор автопортрета в мундире и так далее; (и, конечно же, здесь, в этой главе, он охотник и поэт, который 'не свеж и не молод'); 'Ловчая повесть, или картинки с выставки', где он Ильич Паламахтеров, 'неподкупный свидетель и доезжачiй своего практическаго и безжалостнаго времени', и где он воображает сцену из этнографии девятнадцатого века, в которой принимает участие его прадед; 'Картинки с выставки' (9), где он наблюдает происходящее на улице через окна кадетской школы; см. также другие подобные части книги, 13 и 16. Каждая из них написана с точки зрения автора, но стилизованного автора, т. е., опять-таки не непосредственно меня. Яков — поэт, художник, мечтатель, представитель интеллигенции, рожденный и выросший в городе. Он уже взрослый к моменту своего приезда в Итиль" (327). Яков также играет важную роль в структуризации сюжета, поскольку именно он убивает Илью в знак отомщения за убийство своих собак последним.

text: In ancient Russia, a sloboda referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, sloboda refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
